The dispute in the Irish ranks has caused a good deal of puzzlement amongst members generally. mainly on account of the frequent use of the pnrase "Bantry gang." It may, therefore, be explained that the Healysand Sulltyans hail from the shore:.
of Bantry Bay-, and that, as they are the predomin- ating inflirence in the anti-Sextonite party, they are looked upon as the leaders of the present move- ment .

The Irish Nationalist members were on Monday conspicuous in the House of Comneons by their absence. They sat continuously in one of thecom- mittee rooms, only entering the House to take part in a division. Mr. Gladstone on more than one occasion looked wistfully to the bench usually occupied by Messrs. Sexton, M'Carthv, Blake, Dillon and Healy, and plainly showed by his eager glances at the Irish leaders as they entered the House his anxiety that differences between them should be adjusted.

One of the most curious incidents of the meeting of the Irish party on Monday was the fact that the Currans pere et fils took opposite sides of the vot- ing. Tom Curran, as Mr. Curran, junior, is famil- iarly known, is a strong Ilealyite, and he does not hesitate to give voice to his opinions ; but Mr. Curran, senior, sides with Mr. Sexton. Before the question was put from the chair an appeal was made to the younger man to consider his position, but he indignantly replied that he was present at the meeting as a member of Parliament, not as on of his tether, and he should exercise his free- dom of action. " Sligo," said he, "is entitled to a vote, but Kilkenny is also entitled to speak, and if I obey parental dictation in this matter Sligo will have two votes an Kilkenny none?

Mr. Gladstone in the division lobby on Monday afternoon, gave a striking evidence of the self- forgetfulness, approaching almost to recklessness, in matters concerning hi health. He deliberately seated himself with his back to an open window, and remonstrated with Colonel Nolan, who was sit- ting beside him,on insisting that the window should be shut. Mr. Gladstone is always bareheaded in the division lobbies,where the chances of catching cold owing to draughts are very great. Sir William Harcourt is always covered in the House, except when speaking and in the lobbies

The company which gathered at Barnards'-inn Hall, on Saturday night, at the invitation of the Society of Friends of Russian Freedom, "to meet Mr. George Kennan," was a distinct proof of the success of the society's work. Five members of Parliament were present—Mr. Pickton, Mr. E. J. C. Morton, Mr. W. Allen, Mr. T. Lough, and Mr. Byles. Amongst the Members and visitors were Miss Desba Stretton, Walter Crane, Dr. Todhunter, Belfort Bair. Mr. Wm. Clarke, Mr. Stanley, Mr. and Mrs. E. R. Pease. Perhaps the chief centres t 4 inZerest—ol course, after the guest of the evening—were Kra- potkin, Stepniak, Volkhovsky (ex-refugee from Siberia) and Techaikovsky.

Mr. Kennan gave a heart-moving little address, during the delivery of which be could not conceal his own emotion. He declared his purpose of de- voting the remainder of his life in the cause of the Siberian exiles, whose misery and unmerited suffer- ings he had exposed to the world. The Russian Government hoped by its standing army of soldiers and its lying army of policemen (this was a charac- teristic touch of humour) to keep out of the im- perial preserves the disturbing influence of progres- sive ideas; but this policy was foredoomed to f i ailure. Mr. Kennan's s a striking personality, and a decidedly military beating accorded well with the tone of stern determination in which he told his Learers, amidst sympathetic applause, that he would not lay down his work while life remained in him.

The presence of Dr. Dellinger in the pulpit of John Wesley's Chapel, on Sunday, is an event of greater significance than appears on the surface. For this profound microscopist and evangelical teazher is one of the most uncompromising devotees of the Darwinian hypothesii now living, and if, as at one time seemed likely, the Methodist Church bad invited him to choose between evolution and orthodoxy he wculd not have hesitated/ for 3:non:lent . But the Mettiodizt Church, instead ci looking askant at his perilous views, has delibe- rately relieved him of pastoral duties in order that he may devote himself entirely to scientific re- search, while still retaining his ecclesiastical rights. He is only fifty-two but has already con- tributed a son to the public service, Mr. Percy Dellinger being Professor G f History and Metaphy- biC3 at the Lahore Government College.

'gr.lzel, whose manly protest on behalf of tlio laboring classes against the prOclamation of the Duke of York's wedding day as a public holiday has gone far to dispose of the question, is one of the youngest members of the House, being only in his t wenty-fifth year. Be entered Parliament in 1892 as member for Kirkcaldy on the death of Sir George Campbell, and signalised the first few months of his Parliamentary life by a motion in favour of the establishment of a Department of Labour. Mr.Da!- ziel is a tall, dark, athletic-looking young man, an: ia as ready with his pen as with his tongue. He is London correspondent of the "Scottish Leader,' the Rome Rule paper established in Edinburgh to counteract the political views of the cnioniw, " Scotsman."

Uarold 111 Hilton, the winner of the open golf •cbfituptesuAbip, ig it well-built, pleasant-lookina young fellow of 94. He is a Liverpool man, and acquired much of/his proficiency in the • game on the lloylake links when quite a youth. When he first enteredfor open competitions, his oiler rival soon became aware that they had a formidable op- ponent in young Hilton. In 1890 he reached the final of the Ataatenr Championsliip,at St. Andrew's. in 1892. he played in the final at Sandwich. but he did not shape in his usual goal form and was beaten by Mr. J. Ball, jun. In October last he car- ried off the open championship at Muirtield from the very best exponents of the game in Great Britain. His driving is powerful an,i straight, and his placing most accurate ; in fact, his all-round play is wonderfully good.

While Mr.Chamberlian on Tuesday night, with extraordinary heat and violence, and in a crowded and excited House, was foretelling religious perse- cution as acertain consequence of Home Rule, the Peers' Gallery, in contrast with other parts at the House, had but one occupant, Lord Plunkett, the Protestant Archbishop of Dublin. His Grace must have listened with amusement anti incredulity to Mr. Chamberlain's predictions, inasmuch as a short time ago, addressing a synod of his own clergy in his cathedral in Dublin, he had stated that while be was strongly opposed to Home Rule he was con- vinced that all idea of religious persecution ty an Ii jab Parliament was an utter absurdity.

Mr. Tim Healy nearly scored off Mr. Courtney Tuesday night. The az-chairman of Committee, aims at being scrupulously professional, dogmatic and a: Curate. Mr. Healy criticised tte wording of an amendment proposed by Mr. Courtney. in which the words" abrogating an organdation "occurred. An organization," said Tim "cannot be abrogated c2:01 :nay abrogate a right—you m ust Effcct an orga.nizaofl. At least so it appears to my more Iriah mind? The Bowie laughed consumedly while , Tim.cast a scOrri glance towards Mr. Courtney, ful Sir,ll..Jame., Mr. tii;amberlain, Jesse Collings, and 'the otherliperior petu,ns on the Liberal Unionist A 'bench.

A model which you may like to copy is a prcry bodice midi of black satin in the eroes•over sqle, end mounted on a tight-fitting !Ming. The banging shoulder frills are of black guipure lace. • The alvirt is composed of five flounces of the face mounted ou a ball-dived foundation of black sateen. ' It is not an expensive dress, but is rather a novel one. A geed silk-faced satin may be purchased from is. a yard and upwards, and the amount ne,cevaary for this bodice is &yards of material tl2 inehts wide.

There is something fascinating in the possession of new millinery (vhich few cf us ean resist, and this Lesson every kind of s'yle and shape appears to me to he equally fashionable. llead-geur has only to be becoming, and it will be dubbed fashionable without any question. One of the pettiest confections I have seen for some time was a large hat of gold.coloured Tuscan with a soft frill of cream lace falling over the brim. This.was draped with net, and had black wings both at the front and at the back.

I have just seen a very lovely little bride's gown of delicate Swiss intuilins. The skirt, sleeves, and vest were of the embroidery, while the rest of the bodice was made in crossover style of plain white muslin. The shoulder cape intended to be worn' outdoors, is also entirely a the embroidery. A' more simple and effective little gown it would be hard to find Indeed, I often wonder at the foolish pride which induces many girls to spend pounds of hard-earned money on on elaborate wedding gown, which is a veritable "white elephant" to them directly the eventful day is over. . .

Another very pretty hat was of rainbow straw, ornamented with a windmill bow of pale pink and blue ribbons. Under the brim was a row of pink and blue rosettes made entirely of bob 4 ribbon, which are very becoming. This dainty hat was bound by an edging of black velvet strings coming from under the brim at the back.

Amongst Redfern's fashion for June is one I would gaily and gladly wear through a good six months of the year; it is delightfully adaptable, ).nd would with equal appropriateness, grace a boating party or an afternoon fis.e. Over the shoulders is an admirably chapel collar, and the skirt is cut on an effective principle opening up each side, and obviating all necessity for seems. This should be worn with one of Redfern's batiste shirts, tucked in the front, fitted with a turned down stiff collar, and a chic little neckiio to match.

Overwork and Underwork. Every one has heard of the danger of overwork, yet few understand just where the danger lies. A man can hardly overwork himself if he takes care of himself in other respects—secures a normal amount of sleep, breathes pure air, takes exercise, and eats food mode- rately. The main trouble is that the man who is over- working is violating fundamental eneditions of health. He burns his candle at both ends. With due care,a man of good heredity is capable of safely doing an almost incredible amount of solid wot k. Mr. Gladstone at 83, with no show of weariness, carries the weight of the British Empire. The celebrated 'Jehn Wesley did more wr tit than almost any other man of the last century ; hot he observed the laws of health, and still active, r2aehed his piv,hty:eiLhtli year. Much of the so-called overwork IS the overwork of worry, care, anxiety, and haste. These make the severest draft on the vitality of

div.head: EXAMINER, SAVURDA Y, JUNE 17, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAVURDA Y, JUNE 17, 1893.

the system. We seldom hear of a Quaker dying of over- work, and yet they are a very industrious people. The pupil ,who has prematurely broken down in his studies might have gone on under even heavier loads if there had been nothing to fret him in his home surroundings, and competition, examinations, and scholarship mark- ings had no place in our school system. The fact is, work, and plenty of it, is healthy in a high degree. And this leattli us to say that a lack of work, with brain or hand, is highly injurious. Uoderwork may be as harm- ful as overwork to the brain if not to the body. Nations living in conditions in which the means of livli- hood come almost without effort are in every way feeble. Close confinement in prison tends to idiocy: Further, where the mental faculties are not called ifit• action, the moral al• o lie clormant,and the lower pros epiitii s become all-contrehing. In all ages the corrupticn, ot the WO r classes are duet) this fact. Few worse t imp! c .11 befall one than to have nothing to do.—' Youth's Competitor,.
"I will see lifin," sum said. "Miss Myner can- not be moved under a day Or two". and Lord Dark. wood is her einili:oyer.- I must tU hlm ' .

She descended to the mogiiingreom. Lord Darkwood arid his daughter Were together: She was sullen,-having just received a reproof front her father for not j0P0,,,,' her companion and winning the favour WAliss-icorreys by her devotion to Gwen.

rhe mistre,,s o.f Beeehmont. swept into the mom iicbJy drCSSetl, iuperb in her ,beauty and hauteur, anti the margnis who :looked .none the •,worse for his nocturnal visit to the ruins, stood up, :hewing low befote her.
At sight of Min, Miss Norreys's look turned to stone,.
She WM always pale; now every vestige of colour drifted out of her oliye face. Her brown eyes dilated in a strange terror, an awful emotion that swept over her soul like a devastating tornado.

Lin‘d Darkwood, his head bent 1 in a reveren- tial bow, saw vothin„..o. of the effect of her momentary glimpse of his face. The Lady Georgina had turned to a window in her sullennesS, and also saw nothing of it.

By the time the tnarquis fixed his gaze upon Miss Norreys, the lady had obtained control over her- self. But she was still white, and thas strange terror still brooded in her eyes. She moved grace- fully to a seat, seeing nothing in a momentary blindness that had come upon her.

Lord Darkwood's soul swelled within him as his eyes dwelt.upon her marvellous beauty. He made haste to account for his visit by thanking his hostess warmly for her kindness and hospitality to his daughter and companion. "[s Miss Myner seriously injured?" he asked. "Not serioutly, yet she ought not to be removed for a day or two,' said Miss Norreys, in a sweet contralto voice, that was pure music. "I must request you to allow her ,to remain for the time mentioned. She shall have, every care, as I need hardly assure you." " Certainly, ' said Lord Darkwood, "she shall stay. She is a dear, sweet girl, Miss Norreys, ind my Georgina is devotedly attached to her. They have not been separated for months. Geergina will feel her friend's illness."

"Will not, the Lady Georgina favour me with a visit se long as Miss Myner .remains?" inquired Miss Norreys, courteously. . Lord Darkwood, turned his face towards his daughter, frowning darkly upon her, and com- manding her in every ill-cut feature to accept the invitation thug extended.

, And Georgina acceptail it. "I will have your maid send ,over whatever you may require, Georginu," said her father, pleasantly. "Misa Norreys, you are ten kind to my little girl and to her 'friend also. Miss Myner is a lovely girl, and I am glad to hear that you do not consider her in danger. Having relieved my anxiety, I will not prolong my stay. I will conic again, and as often as you will allow me, to inquire after my dauglo teris young companion, who has greatly endeared herself to its."

True to his word, he did not ,prolong his stay. Miss Norreys inviteg him to call again, and he went away. - As he rode 'down the beech-shaded avenue, his whole being in a tumult, he muttered— ' " I have found at last the peerless worn:tit I mean to marry llt her at • first sight-4, who thought never t. ye again ! Beauty, wealth; and rank all combined in one person. She is not over twenty-five, and the most royally- superb Woman living. She shall be mine I I have never failed yet in aught I have undertaken. I shall win her for my wife ! llail to the future Marchioness of Darkwood I" He rode on gaily, joyful over his anticipated triumph. As the sound oh his horse's hoofs died out on the avehuh; Miss •'Norreys sat (lowa again, and one more q.l)Jerving tlgni Geggina would have noticed her returning pallor, and would have heard her whisper to herself.: .." Alai dreaming? What does it mean? He here—he 1"

But the Lady Georgina Charteris did not note the agitation of her hostess, nor did she hear the whis- pered questioning that fell from her lips. Tinuirl, sullen still, was staring from the window after the retreating footsteps of her father upon the avenue. Her good nature, which had once seemed habitual, often yielded to sullenness in these days. Pros- perity had not had a beneficial effect upon her. Miss Norreys had ample time to indulge in her singular emotion, and to conquer it anew, before Geor"One turned towards her with something of re- Rclvored

Am I to 4o to Marion .now?" asked Georgina, Secretly desiring so see more of the house of which lately slie.had heard so much. "Not just yet, my dear," saidl,Miss Norreys. "1 should like to make your.liettetl. acquaintance, Lady Georgina, since you are to be my guest for a day or two. Permit me to place a chair for you."

, She, did sa, seating ber guest in such a inanher alto kt..ep her OW I 1 face in the shadow. . The Ludy Georgina, flattered and pleased, signi- fied her iileasui-e in making the" better acquain- tance" of her hostess.

" Since my arrival at Beechmont," said Mis Norreys, qnicty, "I have made many ma:paint- ances ; the county people have received me, with grat ciyrdiality. I tun sorry net to have mitt your father and yourself until to-day, Lady Georgina. Will yotz tell me something about yourself?" and she wildcat winninaly, regarding the girl with a fittteraig interest. "Are you an only chiltly,my dear ?" "1.7f:6, lam atronly child," the exclaiined. "I am the heiress apparent tif Dunhohn, Castle and manor, and to my father's title. If my father should not marry again, I shall be Marchioness of D.irkwood in my own right." "You have a noble destiny before you, Lady Georgina," said Miss Norreys, moving a little nearer to the fixii and holding& hand-screen before her fate. "Has-your father long been in possession of. his present title ?" • • 'Only some six or eight months," answered; the Lady Georgina. There was a brief pause. One looking ,at the. pale olive face shadowed hy the hand-screen would liave44hought that Miss Norreys dared lutially-ask the next question that arose to her lips. -But pre- sently the said, and her tone seemed ',careless,

" Who anti wliatwas your father before he be- came Lord DarkwootL my dear? Pardon my curiosity, but I have spellittiOnany years in India that I know very little of the great families et Eng- land and I would like to know well rny nearest neighbours." "Oh, certainly," said Georgina, delighted with the opportunity of tallibig of herself and her family.",' My father was formerly Captain Tollish, of Her Majesty's array. I was Miss Tollish, you know."

As the former name of Lord Darkwood fell from his daughter's lips, Miss Norreys started- In spite of her great self-control, in spite of the fact that she had expected to hear that name, its .very sound caused her a renewalof that fierce and terrible a'gi- tathin that the sight of him had aroused in her. The screen shook iq her-hand ; her face was drawn atd wil4e ; a tortured look flared fratn,linr dusky eyes. Georgina was too.drell and stolid, At.e.absorbed in herself, to, heed these signs of uncoutrol'..Able MO. ti'ou and to 'make deductions therefrom.
," Captain .Tollislx," repeated Miss Norreys, in a voice that was stritngoly rnaglienotand sharpened. " ‘Vhoinl did lie sue.coo,l': The- old lord—his uncle?"

"You know of the family, 11610." eriod Geor- gina. " You know that tho old lord was his uncle ? " "Every. patriotic Briton studies 'Burke's Peer- age,' " replied Miss Norreys. "1 knew years ago that there was a Lord Darkwoodi and that he was Solie ifs dead ? "

" ITe• died ten years ago„'" answered Georgina. "He was a haughty old lard, and he hated my fathes- and my grandfather, because my grand- father changed his family name of Charteris to Tol- lish, his wile's name. HA WAS terribly proud, was the ad marquis." '4. Who succeeded hien!" asked Miss Norreys, almost in a whisper. "His son, Edward Charteris." There was another dead silence. Miss Norreys's Jace gleamed white and tortured behind her kand- screen. Yet she presently spoke again with an assumed indifference that passed for real.

"And your father, Captain Tollish, succeeded not the old lord, but the lord's son, Edward Charteris ? Tell me something of him, Lady Georgina? Was tdurard Charteris married? When aud how did he die?" _ _ _
She held her breath in her anxiety and suspense for the answer. -

It eameparelessly enough, yet every word plereed the listener's heart like a thrust of a hut Damastmi- blade. "The last Lord Da.:k Wood ba.C11.004.? " said the Lady Georg Ula. " 10 held his title •or tenyears, and was a grave, reserved man, the caStle ikervants sayortto looked after.hik tenantry, ana

was adored by his dependents, but who cared nothing for society. He hated women as badly as he hated my father. You see that he and my father were friends in their younger days, but they had,'s frightful quarrel, and became bitterest enemies. The late lord was fond of yachting, and came to his death last year by being wrecked in the Mediterranean. So, as he was dead, leaving so heir' my father succeeded him." "Wrecked ! Lost at sea !"'•

How strange that svieet, low Voice sounded. "Yes," assented Georgina. "He was lost in the' yacht Sylphide. The account was all in the news- papers at the time. ".1 was then on my way home from India. I did not see the newspapers. I never 'even knew that Edward Charteria had become Lord Darkwood."

There was a thrill of anguish in those tones that even Georgina noticed now. She showed her sur- prise in every feature of her round, Dutch face. "Did you know Edward Charteria; Misa.Nor- rays ?" she cried. "I? I know him? How could I know him ?" said Miss NorreyP, more calmly, holding in her emotion with an iron hand. Why, my dear, I have spent more than half my life in India. Had It not been for papa's death, and his desire that I should return to my native land and find a home, I should have spent all my life out there?" "My question was vary foolish," admitted Georgina. "You can't be over twenty-five at the outside, Mies Norreys, and you spent pore than half your life in India, so how could. you have known Lord Darkwood For he never went to India, lam sure. I beg your pardon for my allu- sion to your age. I fanci d that you spoke, you know, as if you had known something of the Charteris,family." "The late Lord Darliwood never married," said Miss Norreys, more to herself than I,n, her guest. "He lived alone, and perished at sea ina storm. Strange life and death r " Yes, they were strange." • - • "I found the cards of Lord 'Darkweod and the Lady Georgina Charteris one. day upon my return from a drive," said 1‘.16a Norreys.. "I had heard something\ of the family, and I entiposed Lord Dark- wood. to be that lord who has just died, and I sup- posed you to be his daughter. I had not positively known,of the old lord's iie-ith, butt knew his age, and deemed his death probable, and thought that his son succeeded him.'

Ah, yes, she had thought all this, and had feared and dreaded to meet Lord tiara wood, even while she felt a strange eagerness and lenwing to look •upon his face. he had called at Dunhohn Castle In that same fear, and dread, and longinc,fand he news of the late lord's death had come upon her in an awful &hock. The sight of the present lord's face had been an equal shock, and the two together were almost Haire than she *mid boar.
"I should have thought that you would have been glad to leave In4ie, Mists Norreys," said Georgina. "1 won dn't live there for a mint of money."

"lc wmi my lom9 replied _Miss Norreye, simply : father and my friends were all there. I wish I had never left it," and her tone grew sud- denly passionate and as suddenly &cued again. "Excuse me, my deaf. I fear I have fatigued you. Allow me to show you a room where yott can lie down an., rest after the morning's excitement. But, first, you have not spoken. of your motheT. Is there no Lady Darkwood ?"

"No; my mother died years ago. There has been no Lady Dorkwood for many years. The old lord's wife died young. The late lord, his son, never married. I hope there will no Lady Darkwood until I come into the tible.."

Miss Norreys laid down her screen,, arose,. and courageously requested the girl to accompany her. They proceeded up the grand staircase, with. its freqgant landings, its niched statuary, its carved baltlfitoade; to the.upper hall. The hostess led her guest to a room Oita further end—a pretty parlour overlooking the heintiful gardens. _adjoining the parlour were bedrooms bath,. and. drAting room, "1 lope you will !Sake yourself comfortable here, Lady Georgina," said Miss Norreys. "our maid and your box will be sent up as-soon, sa they arrive. My house and servants are at your dis- posal, so pray call for anything you may desire." The hostess with a smile withdrew, proceeding to her owe apartments. The bedchamber was occupied by Gwen. Miss Norreys passed into her sitting-rooms and locked her doors. Alone: her forced calmness forsook her. She fell upon her knees by a ()ouch, and give way to such a etorm of anguish and despair as could only have COMO from it passionate eoul. in uttenex- tremity of suffering. "Heaven' help .me !" she moaned' piteously: "Leaven pity nee • What shall I do? Oh, the bitterness of (lsoth has oolue in life. •Ii I could die —if 1 ceii• ild only diet " The tears poured down her cheeks in'a wild rain. Not for years had she wept like this—not even when her indulgent, loving father bad died a year or two before ut India. She gave herself to an tittee abandonment of grief, and lay at last weak aid spent ..and eltnost lifeless upen the carpet, looking like a deadiweirsan..; When once mere she gathered strength to rna,- shal her thoughts, with her dusky head lying against the side of the couch, and her eyes staring wildly and despairingly straight before her with unseeing gaze, she muttered— •

" Fabian :Cellist) here I I %vender that I did not drop at his feet in:a-swoon. Strange that be did not suspect that he-had seen me before. Am- Iso changed? Ile looked into My eyes • and did not remember them, flo looked upon my features, and his memory never told him how often he lied looked upon them before. Fabian Tollish here I•It is fate i that hinnied our live/sou near together again. after these Years !" • Sho lay long in that 'despairing attitude, thinking thoughts like these-we have set down. The. olive face was blanched now to a white pallor, the-dusky eyes were terrible in their expression of pain- and torture. The clock, ehimed the half-hour thrice, and she paid no need. She was only roused; at last by a knocking upouthe ntner door, and even then she was too utterly wearied to answer it, and Nays, stole allay, fancying that her mistress slept.. "i wish that I had not returned to England," murmured the lad.y. "I had learned a. sort of patience out there, I had !earned to bear my life, and now I must learn anew those lessons lbelieved I had learned for good and all. But how, shall I meet Fabian Tellish and not betray myself? What fate brought use to his very door? Is. it that. X may be reieugedi upon hint for all that he has te made me euff r t!' Her noble gtowed with suddetr heat. This new idea see , utterly to take possession of her. To be reveng „impels Fabian Toilish wotdd give new flavour to hr existence, would give new im- pulse to her energies, would be something to live for.

"That is she cried; "I will be revenged upon him. lie wrecked my life. Oh,. that I might wreck his! He does not suspect that he once knew me. Lvbill plan and work, out. a complete revenge." She spranrup and ran to a mitrori, and contain. plated her reflection tvith burning..eyee. Even shas without a shadow at sanity, could not help appreciating her gulped) and wonderful beauty. Lord Dorkwood, when Fabian, 'follies, bad been noted as.amadmirer of bpainty,aud..this dark love. liness was, of the very type,. to, win his deepest admiration. _ _

She•was thinking thus, looking upon herself as, if she had been a painting, or a statue, when Nays& again. knocked. Miss Norr.eys went to the door. The Ilincloo's calm eyes detected traces of that mighty agitation in her Tnistress's face. Its lingr. ing. pallor, swollen eyelids, and still quivering bps !chi of the great storm, that bad passed over her. Naya made no comment, althougn her mistress mover sighed but that the maid's heart ached but she advanced into WI room, inquiring if she: were wanted. .

Miss Norzeys replied in the negative, an Nays reluctantly eturned to Gwen. Before the luncheon hour the Lady Cnoorgina's maid and box arrived from Dunhohn Castle, and the young lady occupied herself in exchanging her habit for a fresh toilette, which her father himself had selected from her wardrobe, anti which was, therefore in good taste. Miss Norreys called for her guest, and conducted her to the breakfast room' where luncheon was served. After the meal, the hostess exhibited to the Lady Georgina the conservatories, the gardens, the art gallery, and other objects of interest, and after- wards ordered a carriage, and the two were driven through the park, and over the country roads for an hour or more, returning in ample time to dross for dinner. The hostess was constant in her attentions to the Lady Georgina, who felt for her a vivid admiration. Lord Darkwood's daughter dressed for dinner, and Miss Norreys came down attired in ajnaize-eloured silk, trimmed with black lace, looking a very queen of beauty. She interested the girl after Mang in engravings; MIL9iO, and conversation, and tito •one could have imagined how she sickened of the girl't stußidity and inanity during all those long lio,vtr. ._ _ .

div.head: flow to make Shortbread.
div.p: flow to make Shortbread.

Shortbread is generally liked, but,as a rule,it is exiien- sive to buy, and much richer than many care for. Here is a very excellent and economical receipt, simple - enough for the most inexperienced to carry gut :-1nto: 10 ounces of flour rub 5 ounces of butter until fine as breaderumbs, and 24 ounces of crushed loaf sugar. After a few minutes working it will become a thick paste. when it may be rolled out the third of an inch thick. To perfect this, the oven must be slow ; it will take about half an hour to bake, and should be quite pale when done. Oatmeal shortbread can be made in the same way, Ene oatmeal taking the place of half the flour.

Restoring Faded Ink. Writing which has faded either from Parchment or paper, whether from damp, immersion in sea-water,the action of sunlight, or friction, can be more or less com- pletely revived. (a) Wash. in warm water to remov, salt if the paper has been immersed in sea-water, and then soak in a weak solution of gallic acid—say, 3 gr. to the cz- (b) Wash in clean water and soak in a solution of protosulphate of iron, 10 gr. to the oz. (c) Apply a a solution of potassium-ferro-cyanide, slightly acidulated with hydro-chloric acid, with a brush, when the writ- ing will appear blue, if any iron is left of the original ink. (d) Slightly damp with water the faded writing, then pass gently over -with a brush which has been lightly moistened with, hydro-sulphuret of ammonia. In a little while the writing will appear black and legible. On parchment the revived writing will retain its colour.

div.head: AUTHOR'S SLIPS.
div.p: AUTHOR'S SLIPS.

Someone who reads books " by the critical card "has presented " Cassell's Saturday Jountal " with a list ol well-known writers' slims. Defoe's mistake is well known, but it may not be every reader of • Robinson Crusoe,' per ha ps,who rt fleets on that particular passage where Crusoe strips and swims to the wreck, and then fills his pockets with ship's biscuits. Coleridge, it would seem was more of a poet than an astronomer. for he makes the " horned moon" at sun- set climb above the eastern bar. .

Dickens, too, gets a new moon up in the east at early evening. while Mr. Walter &sant, in •• Children of Gibc.on." has a new moon rising in the cot as early as two o'clock in the morning. Thackeray speke of Clive Newcome as having a" beau- tiful moustache and whiskers," while the twist made the hero a beardless youth. In The Nevrcomes," too,Clives asks, in 183—: "Why have we no picture of the sovereign and her august con- sort from Smee's brush ? '"fhere was no prince consort till 1840. Anthony Trollope makes one of his characters come up the street whistling with a cigar in his mouth. We recommend anyone who thinks the above question possble to attempt the feat himself. Ouida's " Penchatit " for Making her heroes do all/ kinds of impossible things is well known, but one must ' " kick "when she gives Wanda's lover a library of one million volumes in quite an ordinary building.

div.head: CHINESE UAMBLE RS.
div.p: CHINESE UAMBLE RS.

, The front or principal room is a very large one paintings decorate its walls, and a number of very handsome Chinese lanterns are suspended from the ceiling. Long rows of small tables are on each side— a crowd round every one of them.At the foot of every table sits a pale, hollow-eyed cadaverous looking in- dividual, with a countenance so perfectly expres- sionless he might be a statue, bet for the few Words that drop from hi a lips of stone and proclaim his profession—gambler. In front of him lies a quantity of copper cash, or round coins with holes in them, a tea cup, and two small pieces of wood, like Joss•sticks. In the middle of the table is a board ; on it are maiked squares with Chinese characters, and at the sides of the boards are slips of paper, with corresponding numbers upon them. The person who wishes to bet takes one of the numbered slips of paper, and places it on the same figure on the board. For instance, It he puts one dollar on number 6, he can double it by covering it with a cor- responding number. The board is filled with slips of panel., and when all is ready the keeper of the bank re- moves from the pile of cash as many as he can cover with the tea cup. They artsstitiftied about under the cup for a minute ; it is then raised, and the cash carefully removed • ne by one wiayl,l4le thin sticks and then counted. Should it come b'ut an even number, all who have betted • n even numbers. win,-:a nd the rest loose. The room is generally fillecito overflowing. I have seen from six to eight bundredeambling at one Ugric in it. Bilfince pro- fcrtind reigns from one end of the place to the ott2er,all in- Olmtly watching the game. I have carefullt Studied their countenances, but could not judge from them who won or lost. The same stolid look on every face, not a muscle moved. Sometimes after losing his ready cash, a Chinaman will slake Us whole stock and trade—and lose. I remember an instance of this reckless gambling mania. A shop close to my house was owned by. a Very respectable Chinaman, a quiet fellow, who had his place well stocked with groceries, wines, &c., and owned one ,p4t,int, a boy of about twenty, as quiet and steady as 'los minter. For a few days his shop was shut, much to the inconvenience of his. neiglibrours ; and on inquiry I found it was the annual festival, and both master and man had attended it. At length, Mr. Lung•leo re-opened, but, to every one's astonishment, he was busy sweeping out his shop and weighing out charcoal and lard to the customers, while the 3 ounger sat leisurely smoking and making up the day-books. It appeared they had been gambling from the time they left home. Lung-Fo had lost to his servant all his "money, his whale stock mud }levee ; ad then having waling wore. he vy,liter,d him- self, and !f he 107 t lie to be Servant to the oilier— and he dil bee. thu, tliere ws.Si;i,vp appestance iit triumphs on the boy's face ; master and sei-vant reversed theft places, with the utmost sawkoid., _

div.head: DARK WOOD.
div.p: DARK WOOD.
A TALE OF LONENIOOR.
BY MRS. HARIUKT Limn. Author of "Her Double Life," " Old Life's Shadows," "Lady Kildare," etc.
CHAPTER XXXIX. BXECHMoNT.

We will now return to Miss Norreys and the two Having dismissed the groom, the fornier ap- proached the Laay Georgina, saying, with a graciows ' yet haughty self-pbasession— ..k am Miss Norreys. If you will come with me into the house I will try to Mike you comfortable, while I render your friend every attention." - "I am the Lady Georgina Charters," replied the girl, superciliously, " ana the young lady who is injured is my governess and companion, Miss Myner. I will go with You; thanks.' • Miss NorreYs bowed her bead and approached herViorse, vaulting lightly and gracefully into her saddle—a daring feat that caused Georgina to open her eyes in wonder. Then the lady led the way through the open gateway, Georg.na following. They rode along a winding path, arched over-by great beeches, and gradually,approached the man- sion, the Hindoo, with Gwen in her arms, keeping in advance.. The Lady Georgina, as they proceeded, survoYed her hostess narrowly. - Miss Norreys was no Medusa, as Lord Darkwood had thought, but a young and magnificently beau- tiful woman, slender and graceful, with a haughty carriage, and a countenance of majestic loveliness, if we may so characterise it. She was a brunette, with a clear, pale olive eom- raexion. with lips vividly a net, and deco. soft. spabbiunnhtnt, beauty, and matchedsuerb in eygesr;ce velvety brown eyes, so dark that they seemen black, set under a wide forehead. Her hair was very S, hseupwerabs u in her manners. She had the air of one used to command.; but she had also a gracious sweetness very pleasant to 4vitness.
"'She would never marry my father," thought the ,girl in relief. "She would never marry a stout, Unhandsome sort of indii."

/iy the time this point of her reflections had been attained they had reached the main entrance of the dwelling, and the Hindoo was disappearing within the .portal. Miss Norreys dismounted, a couple of grooms having seen their approach, and being in waiting; the Lady Geoi-ginst followed her example, and they passed up the steps together. Tie Hindoo lad laid his burden Upon a sofa in the hall. The hall porter and a footman stood looking on. Miss -Norreys • turned to the former. "Carry the young lady up to my room," she said. " Naya is there, and will attend to her. -Say that I will collii3 directly." •
The hall porter obeyed, disappearing up the gram! staircase with C wen.. _

Miss Norreys conducted the Lady Georgina into a luxurious morning rooin; and 'presently excused herself, baying that alo, would send nelvg of Miss Alyner as soon as the latter should recover con- sciousness. •

"Tell her I can't come hp to her," said Lord Darkwood's daughter, selfishly. "I can't do her any good, you know, and I'm not good at nursing. I'm very fond of her and all that, but she is only my companion, Miss. Norreys."

This speech was prompted by Georgina's desire to play the great lady before her beautiful hostess. The girl really did like Owen. How could she help it I Grwou wits so noble, so true, so unselfish, that k person with more ingrained self-love than Georgina could not have helped admiring and lovs lag her. , But Georgina fancied that she would lower her- self in avowing an affection for her hired companion and she had a desire to stand well in the esteem ot Miss Norreys. Her hostess, with a slight curl of her scarlet lips, departed, going upstairs to her own private apartment. Her bedchamber was atorfect bower of beauty. ' Wile soft warm flush of rose-pink wails and up- holstery pervaded the room. A brass bedstead, pollAthed like a mirror, and shrouded in hangings of white lace and rose silk, stood in the centre at the room, and upon it lay Gwen, still white as death, and insensibló. _
Naya, the Hindoo maid of Miss Norreys, a calm- faced, serene-eyed woman past middle-age, whose idol was her beautiful mistress, had removed Gwen's outer garments and placed her in the bed.

Miss Norreys looked down 'upon the girl,- upon the loosened tressea of bronze-gold hair, upon the! thin eyelids threifigli Which theAk showed faintly, , upon the straight I. reek features, and her first thought war, that Gwen was dead. Nava real the thought in her dilating eyes. " She revived when they laid her down, inissy,". she said hastily. - "She drew a long ;breath—so,— and stint her eyes again. See, I will revive her." .: The; liintloti went into the dreesing-rooin, return- ing with a little geld-Stoppered flask. With its contents she bathed Gwen's face, and she let a drop fall between the parted white tips.

The efect was magical. A long, sigliing breath came from the She opened her eyes, and a look of wonder iilled them as they rested upon Miss Norreys. "Do not speax, said the latter gently. "You are at Be.eohinont. I am Miss Norreys. Hush, dear. .Naya, look at her wounds." The ninth)°, with long Grown fingers, gently. turned the girl's face away, and the wound upon her head waii3een "It was a deep out; but nothing dangerous. Nays washed away the coagulated blood from the wound and dressed it with a slip of plaster. " That will do now, niissy, ' she said: "It will he well in a week. Have you no other wound ?" .Nly arm hurts," said Gwen, faintly. The arm was examined. It was found to be terribly bruised, and the wrist was sprained. Nayit applied lotions and medicaments, and Gwen Presently acknowledged herself to feel easier. But the lines drawn tightly about:her mouth and fore- head showed' that she was still in pain, and Naya administered a sleeping potion. Miss Norreys went into her dressing-room, changed her habit, and returned fully dressed just as the medical man of Ditnlielin was usheredmo the bedroom. The physician examined the girl's injuries, in- vestigated Naya's medicament, and shook his head solemnly, not understanding them; but, when he saw that the patient was sleeping peace- fully, he deigned to approve the Hindoo's admin. trations, made one or two suggestions, and departed. The day passed quietly away. Lord Darkwoba's note was received, and arrangements made for Lady Georgina—who made no objection—to stay the night. Gwen slept quietly enough throughout the long hours of the night, patiently watched by Naya, and had not awoke when, early the next morning, directly after breakfast was over, Miss Norreys entered the room to learn how she was progressing.
The lady of Beeohmont drew a chair to tho bed- side, and watched the sleeper with a strange intent- ness. _

"Is she not beautiful, Naya ?" she whispered. "Beautiful as the morning, missy," answered the Hindoo. "You are the golden noon. She is the bght, sweet spring; you are the warm, magnificent summer. I like be.st the noon and the summer." i Miss Norreys looked affectionately into the dark, loving face of her attendant. "You will spoil me, Naya, with your praises," she said. "Do you see a look .of patient sadness about this girl's eyes and month ! Young as she is she has seen trouble. She looks as if she might be the darling of some happy home—she is really a, paid companion to Lord Darkwood's heiress." "She would be a pretty pet and companion for yey, missy," suggested Naya, marking her mistress's interest in the girl. Miss Norreys MO led wearily. "I shall keep her here a day or two, Until she recovers," she said. "By that . time I shall.. probably tire of her, as I tire of everybody but i you, dear old Nays. And yet there is something about her that touches me strangely. As she lies now asleep, there is a baby innocence jn her face that few girls keep to her age. How her mother must love her !” Miss Norreys sighed ; iter haughty face shadowed heavily. , There was a kneel; npon the door. Naya opened it., bringing to her mistress a card upon a salver. Miss 'Surreys took up the card, it bore the name of Lord Darkwood.

div.p: At nine o'clock coffee was served M the drawing' room, and ar ten o'clock, Alias Norreys ordered bedroom candles, and ihe evening was m er. Thl Lady Georgina retired to her chamber, and Alia blorreys, with a long sigh ot relief, entered her onrn apartments.

The day had been pleasant, but the night Woo cool. Fires had not been discontinued' at Beech- mont, and one was now burning upon the marble hearth. Miss Norreys drow up a low chair before , it, and gave herself up to thought. And the gab.' ject of her reflections was the &WM as it bad been in the morning—Fabian Tollish, Lord Dark wood. What was be to her? Where had she known him?' In what way had his life been connected with hers! How had he incurred her hatred? How won her desire for revenge ? • Evidently there was some great mystery in the life of the beautiful' Miss Norreys. What was that tsystery ? .

THE POLICE OFFICES'S. CONFESSION. • At the resumed inquest at Hammersmith on Wednes- day right mocerning the deatk of the woman tound murdered at Wormwood 'Sunned:ls on Wednesday last week, and .irvoonnection with which Police Constabe Cooke is in.Thoustody, Ellen ,Godman, wile of a house painter at Tottenham, ideniilfied the young Woman as her daughter, by a former imAband. She stated that the deceased wag 22 years of ago, and was a single woman. -Or.,iiacksm, recalled, said as the result of the com- pletion of ,the post mortest examinatior,l he concluded that adeattewas due to a fracture °I the skull and lacera- tion of thetrain. There %coca tnuise on the neck, pro- *ably cattssci by the hoed of a boot.—Mr. Haynes,. soli:ritor,diere complained that the alleged confession of the person suspected had been circulated. His client instructedinin to. say that the report was uutrue.—Mrs. Kate Robinson, with whom Cooke lodged, gave evidence that -orithe day/ following the murder she saw him burying something in the garden. Witness alter- wards :PSMOY.ed- the et3,rth and saw the truncheon and whistle. The young woman had visited Cooke at, her house, and they then seemed on good term.—The last witness's husband,,a policeman, stated that Cooke • had tokilhim that the girl could conic in for £3OO. Constable Macdonald stated that on Thursday list Cooke said to him, in alluding •to the crime—" They have not yet :get‘the instrument with which it was done. ltis a good ,jab they did not catch we red-handed."—Sub- anspectur Hatchet gave .evidence as to the confession which he said Cenhemade to hini on Friday last at one o'clock. This was to the effect that after remarking 4'l suppose it is no use trying to get out of it," Cooke went off-to say that on the night in question the woman visited .him his heat, and they •had an altercatiM. Hezontinued :—" Thinking to get out of her way, I went across the Scray.bbs, but she followed me. In going acmes a took my truncheon out of my pocket and put at up my sleeve. When near the spot where she was found, 1-said Are you going ?' She said 'No ;, lam going 'to stop and s.nrov you till Sunday, and then you —yourself.' She then turned her head. I drew my truncheon and hit her on the side o. the head. She fell down and never moved. • I then hit her,• think, twice on the head, once under the jaw. I then placed my foot on her _ neck, 'and kept it there, ' about five minutes. She never moved, but gave a moan. 1. then went back to the prison, and i•aw .'OfEnerKenip, and we were very jolly all night after- , wards. I thought nothing of killing her. I have been .happier since she has been dead than I was before. She was always annoying me, and I was in misery." The Hconfessioncreated profound sensation amongst the, pub- lie assembled in'the coroner's court. ! -Inspector Morgan formally put itrlike statement made to Hatcher by Cooke which witness said he received about half-past seven on Friday ,night ;last. With respect to the evidenN of I identificationowitness said that from inquiries made 'ha .Nvas positive that Mrs. Godman was mistaken in suppos- ing the deceased to be her daughter —in ssumming it, the Coroner said that Cooke's alleged emdession was the most damningv'pike .of evidence, particularly as it. ,showed premsditation.—Alter that jury had consulted for an baur and a half, the foreman said they found a ver- dict of ,wilfukenurder against Cooke, but that he had received great, nrovoCation. There appeared to he some difference of ,npaion against the jury, and they were directed to again retire. On returning a second time, the "jurrsaidthat br a bare majority they had found Cooke guilty of wilful murder, but "with great provo- cation." ¶lhiseidict was recorded.

, A public meeting of the inhabitants of Welling- ton was held in the Council Chamber, of the Town Halton Monday night, to consider what, steps War- rington should take on the occasion of the royal marriage on July 6th. • There was a crowtled ands ienee, and among those present were Messrs. F. Menke, J.P., W. Pierpoint, J.P., S. Wright, J.P.,A. J. Jolley, Lawless, p. S. Burgess', T. 'Morris, A. Woods, J. Shaw Green, W. Roberts, G. Wallineton, W. In starting the discussion, he would so far express his views as to say that he thought July 6th would be in- convenient Flo far as Warrington was concerned. (Hear, hear.) Seeing that they had Bank Holiday in August, he did not think any harm could come, if the meeting • did decide to celebrate the occasion, to defer it until that date. He thought that a large number of workmen ; would be put to considerable inconveseence if Walking ; Day was aftered. (Hear, hear.) At Mit+ t arrington Borough Court, on Monday, 'Richard Gurney was charged with ill-treating a horse by working it in an unfit state on the 4tit inst.,and Thomas %right was charged with permit- ting it to be worked.—P.C. Delahay atated that be saw the first defendant driving a horse attached to a 'bus down Buttermarket-st., on the 4th inst. lie examined the horse, and found on the off shoulder a raw wound; about the size a a shilling. On the top of the choin there was another raw wound. It was sweating very much, and was much exhausted. There was another wound under the rupper. , There were also several old woutuls.--Invector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., corroborated the officer's statement as to the state of the animal.—Mr. Monks asked who was responsible for the horses.—lnspector Dowty said that there was a notice in the stables that the horsekeeper was respon- sible for the horses, but the horsekeeper had to take the responsibility or lose his job. The Chief Constable would like to know how it was that the best horses were sent Latchford way. Ile supposed that it was because there were so many magistrates living in that direction.—ln- specter Dowty said that he had received a number of complaints about the 'bus horses. They were a disgrace to the town.—The magistrates decided to adjourn the case until Monday, so that the manager might be sum- moned.

The Clerlmead letters in answer to inquiries respect- ing the provisions of free places at schools in Runcorri from several managers: Mr. Pritchard of the Holy Trinity Schools said that free accommodation was sap- plied for all infants and 'boys and girls in Standard I. Mr. Simpson on behalf • of the Wesleyan Day school stated that the infant school was tree, but there were. no free places in the boys and girls' schools. Mr. Moss, Clerk to the Runcorn School Board,said that the schools . were entirely free, and the accommodation was as fol- lows Green way-road school, boys. 274, girls. 207, Mill ,Brow infants 124.—Mr. Brandreth said that education was free to everyone who liked to have it, and be con- tended that the Board had no right to pay tor the edu- cation of the children chargeable on the Board.—Mr.' Norman said that unless, they could get the parents to be perfectly indifferent to the school,thephildren were sent 'to. they would have no ground to go upon.—Mr. Handley said that the Education Department could get the School Board to make the school sufficiently large to admit children free.—Mr. Taylor said that if the parent chose to send his children to a denominational school, the Act did not force the managers to give free schooling. To got over the difficulty the hoard must persuade the parents to apply to the School Board, otherwise it.could not interfre.—Mr.Brandretli maintained that the Board stood :n the e lace of the parents to these children, and . that therefore they could demand free education. Ile would therefore move that the children's names be sent up to. the Education Deparvyient, and that the !Board demand free education for the.—Mr. Aaron seconded. • —Mr. Norman thought that they had no gi ound to apply , at all, until the parents were indifferent as to which school their children were sent to.—Dr. Gastaldi moved . , as an amendment to Mr. Brandretlo's motion that the . managers of the schools should :be written to asking ' them to provide free places tor the children in charge of the Board.—Mr. Lee seconded.—The amendment was carried by nine votes to eight. In a further discussion of the queAtion, Mr. Jenkins thouOt that it was impos- sible to dictate the creed Which a poor man might believe. ' It would be hard for a Presbyterian to be bound to send his children to a school to which he objected. The children of poor parents had a right to justice, and the parents had a right to send their children to the school they thought proper, and the Board had nothing to grumble at. If a portion of the district should become so populous as to require a larger eEpenditure than an- other portion of the district, as •in the present .case :Runcorn required a larger expenditure, then Runcorn in its turn Might grumble at that. Was it not illogical to grumble because in the Runcorn portion of the district there was a larger population ?—The discussion was de- ferred until the answers from the managers of the. schools arrived.

div.head: WARRINGTON ANGLER'S ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON ANGLER'S ASSOCIATION.

ANOTHER FISHING GROUND. The committee of the Warrington Angler's Asso- ciation have just been granted by the Manchester Ship Canal Company the exclusive right of fishing in Ow. portion of the old river, between Lymm and Thelwali. The Ship Canal there cuts off a bend of the river nearly three miles in length, which will be practically useless for navigation in future. Sow Brook from Lymm Dam runs into the portion of the river at one end, and a brook running from Statham runs in at the other end. It is therefore full of fresh water and already stocked with fish. Fishing will com- mence there on the Ist July, and it is believed that the sheet of water in question, will make a good fishing place for the members of the club. The Association have also got the length of the old canal, nearly four miles, from Walton Arches to Bob's Bridge at Moore,and during the season between 6,000 and 7,000 matured fish have been placed in the water. This also sn,4uld make a capital fishing ground, as the water at the present time , is perfectly clear. There is, however, some little fear of the water being contaminated when a supply is taken to Wigg Bros. and Steel's Works at Runcorn from that portion of the ground. It is proposed that when the new fishing length has been properly stocked with fish, fishing matches will be or• ganised. If possible it is intended to get as many as a hundred competitors, and this will be the first match of this character that has ever taken place in the vicinity of Warrington. Usually the custom is in such competi- tious, to place the competitors ten yards apart,and allow them to fish for a limited time. The prizes are awarded according to the largest " weight" caught by the com- petitors.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural S'anitary Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. J. Mclntyre took the chair, and there were also present Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector.) THE NUISANCE IN'IPECTOR REWARDED. A letter was submittedVrom the Local Government Board stating that they approved of the payment of £2O to Mr. James Farrington, inspector of nuisances, in con- sideration of the extra services rendered by him in con- nection with the outbreak of smallpox. Slllatita.AL SEWAGE OUTFALLS. A. letter was read froin Mr. Wells stating that he in- spected the °Walls from Twenty Step Bridge to Weston %Ant. He found workmen employed at Twenty Step Bridge and was told that the water would forthwith be passed out of the subway from the syphon pipes, and the conveyance sewage would then be fixed. Nothing further appeared to be done between that and the Run- corn Commissioners' boundary. The Folly Brook syphon was fixed in preition and the tide flowed into the iengili of the Ship Canal between Weston Point and the Bridgewater Docks. The subsidiary works connected with the syphons were in hand. Be observed that the embankment of the Ship Canal was being formed across the entrance of . Delanaere Dock. This would alter the conditions which the sewage, discharged into the Weston Canal and docks was now subject to,f and the effect should be watched. He visited the flats on the End Inst. at low water. He found the sewage flowing from the °titian apparently without interruption ; hut there appeared ,to be a slight increase of the silt, collected in the channel. A boat was moored in the channel, and would doubtless tend to hasten the deposit of silt. He was writing to resident engineers on this and one or two other matters of detail.—Mr. Aaron said that the Ship Canal Company had made a splendid job of the Folly Brook syphon.—This was considered satisfactory. THE WHITLEY SCHOOLS. Mr. Lawson, Warrington, sent a letter to the Autho- rity in reply to the request to close the Whitley Wesleyan Sunday School. He stated that after the strictest inquiry from parents and residents of the township, they were agreed that there was no necessity to close the school as the worst of the epidemic was over. They never allowed the children of any familywhere the feverexisted, to cone to the school. The superintendeut of the circuit also failed to MC why the school should be closed unless it was compulsory. A short discussion followed,and it was decided to call the attention of the medical officer to the schools at Whitley, so that they may be guided by his action.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Adams, in his report, stated that a case of small- ox was reported from Weston Point. The patient was removed to the Moore Hospital, and was going on favourably. The other sufferers from the disease were making satisfactory progress, and would shortly be dis- charged. A case of scarlet fever was reported from Antrobus in connection with the recent outbreak at Whitley. portuc HRALTH AMENDMENT ACT, 2PO._

Mr. Williams reported that a committee had met to consider the desirability of adopting the Public Health Amendment Act, 1890, and they thousht they should adopt it in its entirety. The purport of the Act was to give the Authority a number of powers, such as the cleansing of aslipits, malting of ashpits, making good of highways, and supervision of entrances and exits of places of amusement. It would apply more particularly to townships possessing urban powers, and they were applying for those for 'Frodstiam and Appleton. The subject would be again introduced on July 11th, when Mr. Brandreth would move the adoption of a portion of the Act.

Kno,cles represented the widow and family of the de- ceased.—Wm. Underwood, engine driver at the works, stated that about two o'clock on Sunday afternoon, the deceased was waiting for some waggons,which he had to till.with the chemical waste from the ram' If,: asked Witness to run him a waggon down and voluerd u; couple up the waggon he wanted,to these attached to the engine. Deceased went to the points and then motioned for witness to move, and he did so. He had only gone the length of one waggon 'tam the waggons buttpod against the one which rquired moving. Witness could see that instead of going straight on, the waggons had gene round the curve, owing to the points not having been turned. He found the deceased had been crushed between the buffers or. the waggons, and he died while being carried to the time office. It was the duty of the brakesman Newell to turn the poin!s, and couple the waggons, but he was away at dinner.—By Mr.finowles : Mr. Ileatey, the manager, had told him not to allow any person but the brakesman to work shout his train.—By Mr. Allen : The deceased had pi-erica:3ly coupled and uncoupled waggons without the hook. The deceased asked witness three times to bring him the waggon be- fore he obliged him.—John Lawlev. a workman, des- cribed how the accident riccomd. Hs said the deceased was killed through the waggn going on the wrong line because there was no brakesman tot urn the points.— The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and added a rider suggesting that rules for regulating the driving of engines and moving of waggons should be pulb- fished in the works and strictly, enforced. The jury further expressed the opinion that they would have received material nssistande if 11. M. Inspector of factories had been present.

div.head: JUNE 17, 1893. A WHITSUNTIDE -FLIGHT WITH THE WOODCOCK.
div.p: JUNE 17, 1893. A WHITSUNTIDE -FLIGHT WITH THE WOODCOCK.
(By Mn: JOHN PIERO

Yeslit was decided, nemim contradicente, that this cood Whitweek should Prot be all,)wed to run to waste unutilized. Tommy had pre-arranged it. The thing was cut and dried. We were to start from Fiddler's Ferry on the Saturday afternoon's tide fur New Ferry and thence where the weather and fates allowed. All told our crew consisted of four—the owner, the captain, chief mate and a passenger, a member of the council. Well, after the see-stores were got on board and the ship made ship-shape, we cast off and, under two reefed main- sail, began to beat against a somewhat squally s.s.w. wind and the last remnant of a still flawing tide. Thus the woodcock left her companion, the Primrose, whose captain, forgetting that " There is a tide," &c., &c., still delayed his starting. Many curious glances were cast up the breach to see if the dilatory one was coming and at last we had the satisfaction of seeing that she had turned out. Soon our rounding into another reach hid her from view. Here a freer wind sped us along gaily past smoke enveloped Widnes, and whisked us along merrily by Hale Head and the Dungeon', until. toy Garston, the wind failed altogether and we lay in the doldrums—" like a painted ship upon a painted ocean" —motionless upon the rolling and rapid current—if the reader CArl conceive such a paradox. Anyway we had no proper motion—it was all current produced. Now it transpired that our municipal representative—the City Father—had business in Garston—an appointment. Here was a chance of ridding ourselves of the grave respon- sibility attaching to the safe transport of a municipal -Big-bug. What the Mayor might have done to us bad any mishap have happened to our passenger, Heaven, or the Town Clerk, only knows. Chains and dungeons! If he should gct to know the slippery dangers among which his beloved supporter was landed on that tangle- • strewn shore!

Little did our punt—rowed by the reckless Tommy— reek of the honour and responsibility with which it was freighted! And better se; otherwise it might have got nervous and " kecked.' Now, while this important business was being transacted, part of the Warrington steam fleet overtook us with Councillor Beaton on board. Mutual greeting between the water-parted city fathers. Very affecting. Soon, however one of these has biiiiness of his own to attend to. All his time was taken up.in picking his way over the slippery betangled rocks. This choosing between slippery sea-weed and ' too-too adhesive mud, we watched amusedly until the fast running current had swept us from the view. The said current was fast carrying us to the devil. Let me hasten to reassure the reader: It was not Mephistopheles or St. Dunstan's victim—not the boss who rains St. Mit,irt's hotel—but a buoy of that name. Now "needs must when the devil drives" so, there being no wind, and not wishing to be drifted to New Brighton, we got out the oars and pushed in for Now Ferry. Ere reaching this haven, however the Primrose overtook us in tow of the steam launcti " Wanderer." " Oh! for a Tupperian Pegasus to carry one to the heights of proverbial prosaic poetry and enable one to do justice to a quiet haven and a welcome tea! These delights, though oft experienced, are ever new. But evhrs they are a tit commentary on the mutability of human happiness—being very fleeting. some little distance to the N.B. of us lay the "Iridepend- encia " Argentine iron clad—in pawn as unpaid for, her bells noting the passing watches and her bugle sounding pleasantly over the water. ei lien the sun went down and the gas lamps and electric lights along the dockwalls trical their ineffectual best to replace the loss, when the riding !ausps of the snipping went up, to shine forti the night as the "sweet little cherub that sits up al ft to guard the life of poor Jack "—when a glowing stove and a tight spread awning are cheerily sugges- tive of cosiness and repose, we retire to the rough and ready arrangement that serves us for a couch. Then ensue certain sounds of inharinony—solo, duet or trio. Mostly base music, forte to crescendo. Now, when upon Neptune's watery domain, we must conform to Nep- 'tune's moods—we must be ruled by the Odes, and thus, t hough not lunatics, be controlled by lunar influences. and tides are imperative and tyranical, they call the se,ifarer up at most undomestic hours. Early rising anog be a virtue which we must assume, even if we have it hot. This good Sunday morn the crew did not regard it as a lark, to be rising with that bird—no ! the nightingale for their money. They were in flood's vein and thought that fools alone would be rude to Morpheus and shake themselves from his embrace to " See faint flushes in the East awoken
A ,fig say I for any st,c ea!ry p trt k:x..ept, in bnoon." a a * * " The Mall who would .thus early be stirring must to a spoon."

But the stern exigencies of life afloat, compelled us to be heedless of Hoed and his pleas far matutinal idleness and ruse to breakfast and get a pull upon the falls and the cable and away upon the ebbing tide.. First having transhipped our owner for a passage home in the Prim- rose, he not tieing able to stay with us for the. whole time, so it thus came to pass that the ships oemple- !tient was reduced to two—that is to say, beside the captain, first mate, steward, cook and cabin boy, all four comprised within the irrepresible person of Tommy,. who was all these and everything else by turns, and nothing long. Swiftly through the Sloyne the leading wind bore us past the Umbria then at her meetings, having jest taken the place of her new sister the Cam- pania " then on her second outward trip. By the many interesting sights to he seen on .either hand as we sped by f favouring wind and tide impelled, through the narrowing channel of Liverpool, whose ever restless waters tossed us about contemptuously like the bottle corks and other light and unconsidered trifles of flotsam n among which we were onlras a larger chip. Past Seaconabe ,Eremont, and tripper-haunted New Brighton into the Rock Channel—by the Ark of Noah , ,h.,re stranded upon its sandy Ararat, desolate and for- , lorn—an object lesson to sceptics who should come I hereto have any lingering doubts they,tnav have as to the reality of " that greight conflaggeration o' Noah's 'Flood.' For it is here a solid reality—the Ark I ineax, not the fkod. Another solid reality we passed in the shape of Lesaoe Castle and Lighthouse, only to discover another solid reality in the shape of two too solid sands .barring the way into Hovlake. Seeing this we went in for a spin down channel by Spencer's spit bell buoy and an out to meet an incoming flat, but, as the weather was looking black and dirty to windward, we hauled up again for the shore. Just off the now nearly dry en- :trance to the Lake we let go anchor in about four feet, and proceeded to recuperate, i.e., make up for the defi- ciency in our hasty breakfast. And the tide .flowed and uncrossed the masts of the grounded craft in the Lake. which gives one the idea of scissors •, so we weighed and beat into the Lake among the thickly-moored trawlers. One of the dangers of this navigation is the urgent , need of circumspection in order to avoid the Scilla of the ' floating craft on the one hand,and the Charybdis of their heavy moorings on the other. In this as ii, other cases , a medium coerce is best and attest—if near the vessel you are free of the anchors. The holidays being on,tnade I the harbour even fuller than usual. There were vessels from .Donglas and Whitehaven as well as the Liverpool craft. Gradually shoaling our water we brought up nearly abreast of the Lighthouse and made things snug Torthe night. After tea Tommy lifted up his voice and ! td everyone who was concerned to listen—that is , everybody within a quarter-of-a-mile—that—

"They are all at home, all at home, The kids and servant ton, And the missus looking blue, They are all at home, all at home, And papa's on a ta-ta himself." This from a minor—though trolled in anything but a minor key—was pretty well, and might have lasted longer had I not put him ashore in the punt to stretch his legs as well as his lungs and procure further sea stores—soft taok among others. For a bad appetite is net in the list of Tommy's deficiencies ; he is an excel- lent treacherman.

And now, alone, the ritrietstillness of night gradually settled down upon the Woodcock," and her skipper the beach became deserted of its wanderers,—the child- ren 1-ft unfinished the sandy fortress which was to have withstood the attack of the advancing tide—left it but to dream of it and so renew the happy hours —the semi-detached couples lingered to the last loth to go and loth to part, so long as the waning twilight afforded them an excuse, arid now the light-house throws its warning beam athwart the dangers of this great East Hoyle and over on its other edge the rolling buoy gives out en intermittent tang, while away to W. the Dee light blinks fitfully. These signs of bedtime are not neglected—and Tammy comes home when he can cross the gutter by writhing, what time the receding tide had' left the boat dry, among the rest of her kind, on the inside edge of East Doyle flank. And thus in slumberous cnntentment passed the darkening hours. Take an inside-‘ peep at the inhabitants of this floating gipsy tent. The boat is decked, with the exception of a long narrow strip some seven or eight feet long by two feet wide, over this iron rafters support a thtck piece of canvas covering the aperture completely. A plated orifice in tile after part of this awning admits the stove pipe. As we view it to- night we see the decks cumbered by everythirm not vi anted inside—anars, oars, buckets—miscellanea generally are depositea!loutside and lashed. And now just lift the corner of this awning and peep in at the sleepers. A swinging lamp sheds its mild radiance around and'enables us to do this. , Down the middle. of

the boat runs a wooden something like a partition—it is the keel box and now serves to keep for each of the two sleepers, his own half share of the room for himself. On the ceilings—the boarded floor—long sacks stuffed with hay—over these again the sleepers, and on these a snug rug. At the feet of the recumbent forms we see the stove, now burning low and ashy. Forward of the mast and the cable teer, a grating in the fore peak affords accommo- dation for one or two more when the ship's full comple- ment sleep aboard. By the way I hardly know what is the full complement of the Woodcock ! She seems to be very elastic in this matter. I have heard thelate skipper say he has been one of eleven sleeping in her. I should say in her and on each other. Personally I have an objection to amateur Black Holes. If lamto be stifled it shall not be voluntarily and not compulsorily without some kicking. I have been one of six—even then there were some tight fits. Here indeed as the tree falls, so it must lie. An attempt at turning over elicits growls, grunts and objurgatory remarks from your too closely Dacke4 neighbours. But even from adversity some virtue may come. This herring-in-a-barrel like packing,is con- ducive to early rising. Even Dr. Walt's sluggard, hav- ing no room to turn" his sides, his shoulders, and his heavy head " would give up his occupation in disgust. Another cause of the sudden exercise of this virtue is when the outside sleeper finds his bed afloat, by the listing of the boat in grounding, and the consequent rush of bilge water to his side. Let us draw a veil over that scene—a thick one to exclude 'any uncannnical lan- guage. if such should occur. (To be continued.)
