div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE QIJEsTION AT WARRDTGTON.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE QIJEsTION AT WARRDTGTON.

The school attendance cases brought before the Borough magistrates by Mr. G. Riley, the school attendance officer, have been of late, very numerous. A number of such cases were brought before Mr. • Robert Garnett, Dr. Starkey Smith, and Mr. E. J. Guest, on Tuesday morning. Several parents were fined, but some cases were adjourned, and Mr. Taylor (P.C.M.), was instructed to see several of the lads, in the meantime, to induce them to attend school. At the conclusion of the business of the court, Mr. Rebert Garnett said he wished to know whether there was any method by which the attendance at school could be iinproved. The cases were so thoroughly disheartening that it was almost impossible to know what to suggest as reasonable and proper to do. In many cases they punished a man for an offence that he was in some respects not responsible for. If it was possible they ought to get the clergy to meet together and put a few cases on paper before them. The Roman Catholic clergy who had a good deal of influence with their people,.. might bring the question up in their schools, and speak upon it. He did not think enough was done in the town to second the efforts of the school atteudance officer, or the magistrates who attended to hear the cases. He was thoroughly disheartened and sick of them,and he should like to be away when the school cases came on. He had mentioned the matter at a committee meeting of the Social Questions Union. and the Rev. J. Yonge and the Rev. W. H. Drummond said they would attend at the court some morning when the school cases were on. He did not think Mr. Riley was supported in the town as he ought to he. Mr. Riley did his work well, but he wanted moral support as well as legal support. It seemed to him that there was no moral influence brought to bear upon the homes and families.—Dr. Starkey Smith thought one great thing was to instil into Pdaleremntisndthsooufgltihteofplavr)wenstosonth3th e they necessity could geto f their education. child- ren to wore, and considered it was lost time the child spent at school.—Mr. Riley (school attendance officer), pointed out that on Monday mornings there were always crowds of children away from school at the pawnshops. They went to school on Monday afternoon and Tuesday, but on Wednesday they stopped at home with the ex- cuse that their mothers had to go to market. When they did go, all they did was to pilfer if they got the chance. Then all went on right until Friday. The children attended in the morning, but in the afternoon the schools were a quarter empty, and the excuse then was that they were kept at home to clean up.—The Chief Constable said he did tiet think there was a town anywhere where there wa so much money earned as in Warrington, and where the people were poorer. A good deal of it was owing to the drink.—Mr. Garnett asked whether the police could deal with the question of pawn- brokers taking pledges from children under 12 years of age ?—The Chief Constable replied in the affirmative.— Mr. Garnett : That is a point. It is very likely we might do a little bit there.—Mr. Taylor thought it would be a very good thing if there was a conference of clergy on the subject.

div.head: ALARMING FIRE AT NEWTON, INJURY TO A FIREMAN.
div.p: ALARMING FIRE AT NEWTON, INJURY TO A FIREMAN.

About six o'clock on Wednesday morning, afire of serious character and of alarming proportions broke out at the glass bottle works of Messrs. C. B. F. Herron and Co. of Newton. One of the workmen when proceeding to his work noticed smoke issuing from the upper windows of the straw store, in which about 30 tons of straw was placed, for use in packing bottles for despatch. An alarm was given, and Mr. J. Rylance, works manager, on entering the store, found a quantity of straw in one corner in flames. The draught caused by opening the door fanned tie flames which shot up, and seized the roef. Mr. Rvlance called assistance, and several buckets of water were thrown on the flames, but they had little or no effect. Seeing that nothing could be done without a good supply of water, word was sent to the London and North-Western waggon works, at Earlestown, and to Messrs. McCorqu ()dale and Co.'s works for the fire brigades. It was a quarter past six before the former received any information, but in ten minutes afterwards they were at the scene of the conflagration ; McCorquodale's engine not turning up until:about seven o'clock. The whole building was then in flames, and on the engine coupling up to the mains, they were unable to get a sufficient force of water. They had then to have recourse to two pits in the works yard. and by this means they were enabled to get a good stream of water on to the flames. It was soon seen that nothing could save the two warehouses, and the efforts of the firemen were directed to saving the reading room and offices, which were in imminent danger, and in this the men were entirely succe,sful. Everybody worked with great earnestness, and put forth Herculean efforts to stem the flames. The fire raged with fearful violence, and before long the roof fell in carrying with it the second floor of the main warehouse, and the flames then shot up to a great height grave fears being entertained that the old cottages ad- joining the works in Gas-street, would be enveloped. The tenants quickly cleared out, but fortunately the buildings escaped. Had the wind been blowing in an opposite direction nothing could have saved them, and the gas works would also have been in some danger. Thousands oat bottles were stored in the warehouse, and a large quantity were stored ready for despatch on the morning of the outbreak, and these were all damaged by the fierceness of the flames, and by the falling del:rig. Mr. C. L. F. Borron arrived about nine o'clock, and directed affairs.

During thS-o-Parations a member of the Earlestown brigade was injured by a falling wall, but he continued at work, and managed to hobble about uutil all was over. On returning to the works, he was examined by two members of St. John's Ambulance, and was recom- mended to a doctor. He was taken to Dr. Valentine's who found he had broken one of the ankle bones, and he attended to the injury. Another accident which might have had serious results happened to Mr. Win. Birkenhead. With another man he was ordered to des- cend a well over 90 feet deep to clear the suction pipes to see if water could be ohta!ned there. One man had

descended, but when girkenhead was going- cEw—u.,lll; rope broke. After falling about 20 feet, he mana.g,ed to grasp a cross tar which supports the pipes and thus saved himself from certain death,"- Whpn rescued he was found to have sustained only slight injury to his side. The fire was got under about 10 O'clock, but it continued to smoulder for many hours afterwards. In- spector Kelly, Sergeant Longworth, and other members of the police force, were present and rendered some assistance. Too much praise cannot he given to the fire brigades, the members of which worked with a will. The damage to buildings, which were completely gutted, and stock, is estimated at about £3,000, and is covered by insurance.

div.head: – FEN FAMMERS AND THE POTATO TRADE.
div.p: - FEN FAMMERS AND THE POTATO TRADE.

A correspondent wrs to the "Daily News :—Owing to the state of the potato market in London some extra- ordinary transactions have just taken place with some of the Fen farmers. Mr. Alderman A. Thorney, farmer, sent 35 tons of p)tatnes of good sample to a London salesman, and after carriage and commission, Szc., had been deducted, the amount remaining for the grower was 12i 10,1., or less than 4. per ton. For five tons a fitrro,!r of Fleet, near Spalding, secured 7s 9d., and Mr. Ranks, a prominent farmer of Gedney Dyke, near Spudding, forwarded two trucks of potatoes, and he was informed by the salesman that he was indebted ttr him in the sum of 7d. on the transaction, the amount not covering cost of carriage and expenses.

RESIGNATION OF ANOTHER NATION- ALIST e.I!EMBER. Mr. Morrogh, M.P. for South-East Cork, has resigned his seat. This step has belt.: taken in consequence of recent events in the Irish party, but it is understood that Mr. Morrogh was anxious in any case to retire from Parliaibent, and that he has merely taken this opportun- ity of carrying out his intention. He is connected with the De Beers mines and other undertakings, and desires to have more time to devote to his business.

Even the Speaker, i [ usually so cool-headed and ready to meet emer- gencies, was not prepared to deal with this un- usual request. He had te turn to the Standing Orders, and there it was found that Mr. HARDIE , was within his right. It was seen that if not fewer than ten members rose in support of a motion for adjournment a division could be de- manded, and more than ten had supported Mr. lisaines proposal. In this way the Labour member for West Ham displayed to his mentors that he had followed their advise te• study the rules of the House—and had bettered their in- etille''icm As to the question which Mr. HARDIE ' . asked there is sotnethiug to be said. .It ito be inferred from what is set forth in the question itself that a number of workmen at one of the Government yards at Deptford had petitioned fcr s°the improvement in the conditions of tliei: labour. For having signed this petition three men had been dismissed, and one of them, ma an old ri Of sixty-five named Edward Pluck—who Perhaps saw nothing in front of , him bit the w orkhouse and the pauper's unifcrm— !oraraitted suicide. In the official answer the _ :i• are admitted, but it was explained that the men were " withdrawn" by a contractor and not by the Admiralty itself. Taking all the circuin- _stances into account, the case appeared to be •.: , v!e-eroinently one for inquiry, and it is not at all * 'iatiafactory to learn that Mr. HARDIE'S action was greettd with . •,_ X People," 14,11 d laughter and ironical cheers." A,, Great THOSE people who have persuaded jeroprrance • themselves that there is no ' ...S.' em"strati"• popular demand for the Local have been rudely disillusionised .'bytke remarkable demonstration which was held ''° Linden on Satniciay. That demonstration Showed tery clearly that, in the great Metropolis ('4 all events, there.l isAt demand, and a very loud —"lend too, for local option. As one correspond- -, , eat has said, tlietathering demonstrated most "nlPletely and surPrisingly the enormous strength of the teetotal party in London. Numerous con- tingents centred on Hyde Park from all Parte.of , London and its suburbs. They were 61;1rn.. rtliarr°%7 and Kilburn, from Islington, Woolwich,‘ ''ataberwell, Deptford; Wimbledon, Croydon, apd IllanY other parts. Almost every kind of tlmper- , „„ 7,"ee organisation sent its representatives, and had 3 banner. The banners and the mittoes they, contained were, by the way, 4,E the ' ast interesting part of the affair) How for instance, is almosf*-: the "hole argument for local option condensed, into the inscription " Oh, the public-house is thear)b,Ori zaa.ll'a cellar, is it ? Then give him the key.„; What was wanted to give it completeness was sup— plied by tile following question and answer : "What, rob a poor man of his beer? Yes, and give him good victuals instead." The question, " Who's boss—the publican or the people ? " was not at all inapposite. The sardonic humour of Some of the demonstraters was displayed in the !arge white flag with a black border, and contain- ing the inscription " This is Bung's funeral " ; and in the wagon carryin, a gibbet on which hung a bottle labe:led " The devil in solution." In Hyde l'ark itself, there was no fewer than twenty plat- 2rmsy and they were all surrounded with an eager throng of listeners. It had been thought by some that the publicans and their henchmen might muster in force to intr educe, if possible, a note of discord, as a set-off against their own collapse in Trafalgar Square. But if this design was ever entertained it was not carried out. The only drawback to the success of the demonstration was ca used by its very magnitude, for while the first detachment had reached the meeting place at five O'clock the last did not arrive at the Park till eight 0 clock. By that time the resolution had been Patsed at some of the meetings, and the demon- strators were well on their way home. Allowing for all drawbacks, however, the demonstration W 53, both in regarct to numbers and enthusiasm, of the mos t remarkable that even London has Vitnessed, and it certainly disposes of the idea, whichlias been zealously fostered in some quarters that the Veto bill is regarded with indifference by tlfi temperance section of the community. '

The Duke f AN interesting character sketch of York, the DUKR of Yosit is given in this. month's " New Review." It ha" bee,-, • 8 nd that that nation is most fortunate which has no history. If the same test can be applied. • ,toan individual the DUKE of Yoax's life must ilh" been pleasantly spent. The reviewer has (4).11131 had a moderate stock of biographical details 43 Work upon. At as early an age as twelve, Prince R°lms entered thc Navy, and up till quite re- • "ntlY most of his time has been spent on board shin. He has served on nearly every naval station the East Indian, the Australian, the South aid he South America,three timeeon the tvorth American and West Indian, and as many More in the Mediterranean and in the Channel, and on board ships of nearly every sort and kind.' RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Present Measrs,g. Handley, R. Morris, and W. F. Soliteld (se.;.). ACCIDLNT TO A CAPTAIN AT RUNCORN. On Sunda, ni.rtriig, about nine o'clock, a serious ac- cident betel DlVid Pugh, of Port Dinorwic, near Carnar- von, captain of the schooner Sparling, of Chester. The vessel and another, named the Archie, were being towed into the locks at the entrance to Runcorn docks, by the steamer Gower, when the rope of the Amide broke the "Lleat" of the Sparling, which struck Pugh forcibly on the side of the head, whereby he sustained serious inter- nal injuries. Blood oozed from his ears. He was assisted to his cabin and Dr. MacLennan subsequently attended to him. From the medical examination it appeared that Captain Pugh was suffering from concussion of the brain, and also from internal injuries. The bulwarks of the Sparling were also damaged.

VICTIMISING RUNCORN TRADESAIRN. Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies at Runcorn Police Court on Saturday. Sarah Ellen Pratt, a in:ddle-aged woman of no settled abode, was charged with obtaining relief by false and fraudulent pretences. Evidence was given that for several days the woman had called upon tradesmen and the residents of Higher Runcorn arid asked for reilef. She represented that she had a child dead in the house and was unable to bury it because she was penniless, and many believing her sad story gave her money. Eventually the matter was reported to the police, who found that her story was utterly false and on Friday night P.C. Gregory arrested her.—The Bench sentenced her to 21 days imprison- ment. ALLECIIID ASSAULT WITH A POKER AT WIDNES. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. J. Birchall, a married woman named Ann Morgan Pear-st. was tarought up on remand charged with unlawfully wounding another woman named Ann Dooley, on the 27th ult. The evidence was to the effect that an the day in question there was a disturbance in Pear-st., where both women lived. After some words had passed be- tween them the prisoner went into her house. She came out again with a poker. and went up to the prosecutrix, caught hold of her by the hair of her head, and then struck Docley several times, stunning her. The wound inflicted was a serious one, and er-sipelas set in. Dr. Hutchinson was called in, and the woman has now re- covered. The prisoner was committed for trial at the County Quarter Sessions. ! div.head: WATER CASK.
div.p: WATER CASK.

Before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele, three dock labourers named George Houghton, James Crossman and Sarnusl Stubbs, young men, were chaiged with assault- ing Alfred Wilkinson on the 6th June. Wilkinson was in charge of the flat Elizabeth, and the prisoners were unloading the boat. Because of previous conduct, he refused to give them a drink of water, whereupon two of them threw him to the deck and forcibly held him there while the third obtained the water. The prisoners said they had been working hard to empty the hold were nearly choking, and were badly in want of a drink. They called a witness to prove that the prosecutor at- I tempted to throw Boughton into the dock and then a scramble ensued. Houghton and Grossman were each ordered to pay costs 6s. 6d.. Stubbs, it appeared had been wrongfully summoned, and he was dismissed. When in want of a CHASTE MA ELEGANT WEDDING Or BIRTHDAY PRESENT go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, High-st .—Advt.

A PRECOCIOUS YOUNG THIEF AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn- Petty Sessions, on Monday, Matilda Hol- land, aged 12 years, was charged with having sttlen a silver chain, a shawl, and a petticoat, of the total value of £1 35., the property of Elizabeth Ann Mason, of 29, Surrey-st. The girl and her father had been lodging at Mrs. Mason's since the 10th of May, and since that date thiartlclee had been missed. On the 6th June Mrs. Mason gave information to the police,not suspectingthat the girl was the thief, but P.C. Gregory ascertained that the prisoner had pledged the whole of the articles at Mr. Lightfoot's pawnshop, and he therefore took her into custody.—Superintendent Atherton said the girl had a bad mother, and Mrs. Mason did not wish to press the ease, being desirous of giving her another chance. Neither of the girl's parents were present, and the Bench said it was evident they thought very little about her.— She was discharged.

ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. On Monday afternoon; a labourer named Michael McLoughlin, of 36, Nelson-street, was seriously injured whilst following his employment at Messrs. Mathieson's works. He was engaged near a large crane, when a heavy iron chain fell on his head, knocking him sense- less, and fracturing his skull. The ambulance vi as sent for, and McLoughlin was conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where he was attended by Dr. Donnelly.

SUDDEN ‘DEAIH AT RUNCORN. Blindly after Wednesday midnight, Wm. Corkin, 50, of Cambridge-rt., Runcorn, died suddenly. His wife, Ann Corkin, states that for the past ten weeks he had been drinking. Be had complained of pains in kis chest I and especially so during the last few trays. They went to WA shout half-past ten on Wednesday niFeht. At hail- past 12 he awoke and got out of bed, hut fell backwards and died immediately.—Mr. Wors'ey held an inquest on the body yesterday morning, and after hearing the evi- dence of Dr. McDougall,the jury returned a verdict that death resulted from failure of the heart's action, acceler- ated by want of food and ex.•essive drinking. LAUNCRINO BANONS AT RUNCORN. , On Thursday evening two niore ot the fleet of fiat- bottomed barges for use on the-Manchester Ship Canal were successfully launched at the Company's ship- building yard at Runcorn. They are 69 feet long, with 14 feet 2 inches beam; the ends being semi-circular, and the side k almost perpendicular. They possess great carrying capacity, and are fitted with apparatus for connecting a number of barges together, thus forming one long train. By this fleet large ships when necessary , can be unloaded in the lower portions of the Ship Canal and cargoes despatched expeditiously to their destina- tion, even if on smaller canals. • The barges are so con- structed as to only draw four feet when loaded. RIINCOR, WODIRNI. TEMTEHANCE ASSOCIATION. A successf44 meet iVii, in connectiwi with the Women's Temperance Society was held in the Wesleyan School, Nelson-st., on Monday. One of the members had offered to provide tea for as many as could be induced to attend The members of the committee visited the houses in the neighbourhood of Nelson-st.. Brunehvick-st., and similar districts, and personally invited the women to the meeting. About forty persons responded. Mrs. Geo. Marshall tnek the chair, and in a touching speech in- troduced Mrs. Mary Williams, of the Chester branch of the British Women's Temperance Association, to the meeting. Mrs. Williams, who is an exnerienced plat- form speaker, soon rivetted the attention of her audience as she portrayed in graphic language the evils of drink, and appealed to them to join the ranks of the abstainers. As the result of the meeting fifteen pledges of abstinenee were taken. After the speakinz, " Afternoon tea," was dispensed, to the evident enjoyment of all present. The committee left the meeting with a feeling of satisfaction that their humble efforts had been successful. div.p: SUPTOSRD SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday, an inquest was held at Runcorn Ririe! Board office into the circumstances of the death of Win. Gibson. aged 37 years, who was found dead in a pit in Wells-lane, Higher Runcorn, on Sunday. The deceased ho had been employed as a farm labourer, had been out of work for some months, and on Friday tic left the house of his brother-in-law, John Burton, 34, Egerton- street, with the intenffin of looking for employment. He did notreturn. On Sunday afternoon he met Philip Taybr, labourer, Higher Runcorn, in Mongbland-lane, whom he informed that he had bad been put out of his lodgings. Ile also complained of being hungry and thirsty, not having had anything to eat for two days. He cried bitterly. Taylor requested him to go to the farm but he refused, and when told to wait where he was until milking time, he replied " I don't know where I shall be then." This was at half-past four, at twenty minutes past five his dead body WWI found in the pond by Thomas ‘Valker of St. John-st.—The jury returned an open verdict. A WIDNES PIIELKAN AND LDS UNSTAMPED GLASSES. On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. J. fireball and Lieut.-Colonel Gaskell, Samuel Hurst, land- lord of the Commercial Hetel, Appleton. was summoned at the instance of Mr. R. Kilpatrick, inspector of weights and measures, for having in his possession and using several glasses not up to the standard measure and nct stamped. The inspector stated that he visited the Sports field, Farnwerth, on Saturday afternoon. He went into the refreshment bars, which were under the management of the defendant, and found that the half- pint glasses were unstamped. There arra 470 glasses in the bars, and on testing them witness found that they were twelve fluid drachms short. The defendant pleaded guilty, but said he had no intention whatever of defrauding the public. The glasses were not those he used on his licensed premises. He bought th.m all from a man named Crossl ey in Manchester that week. He had been in business thirty years, and this was the first charge against him.--The Chairman said the Bench were inclined to deal leniently with the defendant. Taking all the circumstances of the case into considera- tion, they had decided to dismiss the ease on payment of costa.—On the application of Mr. Kilpatrick, the glasses were ordered to be confiscated.

On :Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. .T. Birchall and Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell, Mr. G. W. Allen, solicitor, of the firm of Messuii Oppenheim and Malkin, St. Helens, applied on beliatt.af the Corporation for an order under the Public Health ,Act to compel Mr. James Davies,'Witt-road, to abate certain nuisances in Brown-street, which were injurious to the public health. Defendant denied the ownership of the property —Mr. Allen read an extract from the Public Health Act, which stated that the agent or trustee of the property was liable.—W. Lowe, sanitary ins:rctor for the Corporation deposed that Dr. O'Keeffe said the condition of the pro- perty was likely to cause typhoid fever, or English cholera, especially during the hot weather. The house., were ria habitable. The Bench granted an order for the nuisance to be abated within three weeks. Three appli- cations were made against Mr. Joseph Payne Kershaw, Peel House-lane, under the same Act, to anate existing nuisances on his property in Victoria-street, Edmund- street. end George-street. The Sanitary Inspector spoke to reporting the Nuisance to the Health Com- mittee. Dr. O'Keeffe described the property as being in a shockingly filthy dirty state, and requiring immediate attention, as the nuisance was very dangerous to thobe living in the houses, as well as the pa.s,ers-by. div.p: RAos.

The most disastrous race ever known in connec- tion with the St. Helene Homing Society took place on Wednesday. 2vo fewer than 217 birds were on Monday forwarded to Raynor's Hotel, Ventnor, Isle of Wight, and Mr. Raynor liberated them at noon on Wednesday in a light wind. Only one bird arrived home the same day, and that belonged to Mr. Richaid Dixon. Its velocity was 827 yards a minute. The result is most unsatisfactory, and it is feared that over 200 birds are lost.

The anticipated scenes. at :Widnes Town'Council on the Councillor Bullough 'motion did not take place last Tuesday. Alderman Sadler acted with commendable judgment in withdrawing his motion. Had he gone forward with the subject the dignity of the Council might have become compromised. Councillor Bullough to judge by the expressions which fell from his lips and the expression upon his face was greatly relieved that byegonea had to be byegones.

Of course we arc all pleased that the Duke of York should be marrying an English princess, but personally I can see very little reason for going into ecstacies over the business. The motion of the Mayor of Widnes, at the Council meeting on Tues- day!would in ni) opinion have amply met the case, but if the event has to be commemorated then Councillor F. Neil's proposal was the best that could be made. Any occasion that will provide enjoy- ment for the young and a little extra comfort for the aged,ia to be heartily welcomed, but to go to the extent of making the day a general holiday, those moat to be consulted are the workingmen. There are many who cannot afford and do not desire to ! lose a day's wage, and their interests ought to be I considered. There is not much fun in throwing up your cap and shouting hurrah when the pocket is not lined with a florin or two and the hardy sons of toil will show their loyalty quite as sincerely, following their daily toil as mooning about the streets staring at bunting and flags, or, perhaps dodging into pubs to endeavour to get a quenchor if the weather remains as scorching as we have it at present. Perhaps the men would not object so niuch to the stoppage of the work as to the stoppage of the wages, and Councillor Quinn's sug- gestion is a valuable one. Let those best able, stand the cost of the holiday, if it has to be general.

It is estimated that £2OO to £3OO will be needed to give the treat to the children and the aged poor, and the Committee appointed to arrange for the commemoration,aPpeal for subscriptions. The day and Sunday schools are requested to appoint one representative on the Comtnittee.

div.head: OPENING OF THE ItUNCORN DOCKS.
div.p: THE OPENING OF THE ItUNCORN DOCKS.

• As was announced last Saturday in this journal. Runcorn • Docks were opened on Friday night. The traffic is conducted through Bridgewater Lock, and across a small-stretch of the Ship Canal to the tidal basin. Unfortunately, the deep in the river at the lock is far from a good one, and hence no little difficulty has been experienced in guiding the vessels into the lock. A number of steamers have been stranded near the entrance, viz., on Sunday the steamer White Rose of Liverpool; on Monday the se.lionners Agnes Crag, of Chester, and the Morning Star, of Aberystwith ; and on Tuesday the steamer Harring- ton, of Liverpool, and the schooner G. L. Waters, of Dublin. On Wednesibly Captain Johnson, who has been pierhead master at Runcorn for SOMP years, and has had largo experience of dealing with traffic of ibis descrip- tion, WAS put in charge of the Bridgewater Lock, and it was a matter of great satisfaction to chip owners that Ihe succeeded in " locking" the lot without mishap. Captain Johnson has also succeeded in improving the d. ep to an appreciable extent, and matters may he ex- pected to orotk smoothly in the course of a few days. It may he mentioned that Weston Point Docks are now closed in order that the construction of the canal in that district may be proceeded with more expeditiously. The traffic will be worked vi tt the Ship Canal and Weaver Canal. It is confidently expected that the canal will be open from Eastha.m to beyond Runcorn by the end of August.

A VACANCY. The Town Clerk reported that Mr. John Fitzpatrick, one of the councillors. having been declared a b.tukrupt, had ceased to hold office.—The M yor proposed a resolu- tion declaring the office vacant, and that the same be signified in the manner prescribed by the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882.—Alderman Wareing seconded.— Carried.

THE ROYAL MAR IZIAGE.-A CELEBRATION AGREED TO.

With regard to the approaching Royal marriage, the Mayor proposed a resolution congratulating the Prince and Princess of Wales upon the approaching marriage of H.R.H. the Duke of York, Ka., and H.S.H. the Princess Victoria Mary of Teck and expressing good wishes for the future welfare of the Duke and Princess.—Councillor Quinn seconded with infinite pleasure, because in the, first p ace it gave him an opportunity of showing that , the Irish and Catholics of Widnes were as loyal to the ! Crown as the Scotch, Welsh or even the English them- ' selves. He had the approval of every one of his colleagues in seconding the motion. He eulogised the Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales and expressed the hope that the Duke of York and his bride would have a happy end unclouded life.—The motion was carried unanimously. A letteA.addressed to the Mayor was read from the Counteskef.Sefton, asking Widnes to join in a tribute famtheteuuty. The Mayor said he would reply that. he slteiltbe pleased to forward any subscriptions he peightieceive.—Coundillor F. NVI suggested that they tiggliE ail' further show their feaings with regard to the approaching marriage, by getting up a subscription list ! to give the day and Sfinday school Children a treat and if possible a treat to the aged poor. He moved a reaolu- ! tion to that eff '—Councillor Gough seconded. He did not see that Iti arriage could be 'celebrated in a coli ! better way.— the.,suggestion of the Mayor, it was , resolved to c oder the subject in committee at the end of the meeting. —ln Committee Councillor Neil again made his motion.—Councillor Quinn inquired if it was contemplated making the day a general holiday.— The Mayor : That is for you to decide.—Councillor Hodgkinson said arrangements had been made far hold- ing an united demonstration of the whole of the Sunday school children except the Catholice in August, but he had no doubt that the Committee having the affair in hand would join with the Council for the marriage cele- bration.—Councillor Neil said he should like to add to WI! reselution, that a general holiday be proclaimed.— The Town Clerk said they could not proclaim a holiday but his worship might suggest to the inhabitants the desirability of making the day a general holiday.— Councillor Qninn : And that the United Alkali C >mpany should pay their men a day's wage (Alderman Wareing: Hear, hear, and laughter).—Councillor Quinn added that if the Company would do that they would be showering blessings instead of the ether thing.—Councillor Smith seconded the motion, end said he should like a sugges- tion to come from the Mayor to the United Alkali Coin- pany to give their men in Widnes a holiday and pay 'their wages. (Laughter.)—The Mayor said the matter would be sufficiently public by what they were doing. If the United Alkali Company Wished to do what had been suggested they would be able and willing to du so without any interterence from him at all. He did not think it was either dignified or the place of a Mayor to solicit such a thing from any ordinary company._ Councillor Barlow : If you are going to take that step I would suggest that you include copper works, soap works, &c. (Laughter.)—The May or said those who chose to take th-: thing up might do so.—The motion was then carried and the Council was formed into a committee with power to add to their number Vi deal with the matter. .

I have to report for your information that I have surveyed land for the site of a proposed night soil depot at Moor-lane and Lowerhouse-lane. This land has frontages to two ' roads—Moor-lane (frontage 650 feet), which is an adopted highway repairable by the Corporation, and Lowerhouse-lane (frontage 520 feet), which is private road. The shape of the plot is triangular, with the M. S. and L. Railway on one rile, and the above-men. Honed roads forming the remaining two sides of the triangle. The contents of the land is 5 acres 5 perches, and I value this land at about £6OO per acre freehold, or £3,000 for the site as shown on plan, subject to the Trustees of the Hutchinson Estate obtaining for the Cor- poration a railway siding on to this land at the net cost of the materials employed in the construction of the said siding. The site is well adapted for the purpose it is required ; it is well situated, being central from either W^st Bank or Simms' Cros., and is convenient for farmers obtaining manure, :Itid carting to the adjoining agricultural districts. Lie now said he had consulte4 various authorities on the matter, and he had also had the advice of his worship the Mayor, and under the whole circumAances lie must ask to withdraw the motion. The town's meeting on Monday unanimously de- cided to hold over the celebrations for the royal wedding to August Monday,and also to keep to the original date fixed for Walking Day. This is with- out doubt the wisest decision that could be arrived at, al was, s assuming, of course, that there is to be a celebration.To have thecelebrations on June 6 would• mean two broken weeks;owing to its being almost ha possible to change Walking Day. The Mayor echoed the feeling of the meeting vrhen he spoke against having a procession of children thrbugh the town. is it was within the recollection of most people present,that he Jubilee celebration was celebrated more by fainting children than by anything else. If sufficient funds can be 'raised, there will he a treat to the children of some kind, also a fireworks display at night. Unfortunately..the fireworks will have to be set off" in a different spot to the Jubilee fireworks, as that place has had consider- able attentions from builders sines 1887. It was a splendid place for the spectators, and the park will not equal it in any respect.

Mr. Diggle after a long period of silence on the question of the Intercepting Depots,again appeared at the Borough court yesterday to make a complaint with regard to the Howley Depot. lie complained of being almost poisoned, but he has changed his former mode of proceedings, and yesterday, instead of asking for a summons against the chairman of the Committee in charge of the depot, gave the magistrates an invitation to test with their olfac- tory organs whether his complaint was just or net. They, however, declined his kind invitation, and Mr. !Jiggle will have to continue to thrive on it as litretolore.

The report on the smallpox epidemic which has been presented to the Health Committee by Dr. J. Guest Hornell, is an exhaustive and, from some points of view, a very valuable document. It must nave cost the Soctor no end of trouble to compile. As might be expected, the anti-vaccinationists will had little comfort in Dr.Gornall's conclusions. Be- fore going farther, let me explain, however, to any anti-vaccinationist who may read these lines, that I am not strongly biassed on the sublect.Htiving once in my life submitted to the Jennerian "rite," Lam cpite content to sit on the fence and waif patiently till the report of the Royal Commission on vaccina- tion is issued, and that is confidently expected within the next twenty years. I must say this, liovvever, that it does seem as though the doctors have all the argdnaents on their side—or, at least, all the figures; but then, perhaps ihe anti-vaccina- tionist will retort that they are the doctor's own figures.

Dr. Gomall's report is, undoubtedly, a very im- portant contribution to the controversy. He has not the slightest deubt of the efficacy of vaccina- tion. In one part of the report he says "small-pox is, to my !Lind, the most absolutely certain fact in medicine; and when one knows the erroneous views entertainhd about it, the illogical arguments used against it, and the want of courage and independ- ence of many of the medical men (I do not say in Warrington) in supporting what they know to be the truth, and in carrying out the vaccination laws, one Las little hesitation, in such a case, in throwing off professional reserve, much as I value that. At the foot of the same page that the above quotation is taken from there is the following note ot a rather curious incident:—" I have recently stood at the bedside of a young and healthy man dying of a most terrible attack of small-pox, who, I felt morally certain, would be living now had be been vaccin- ated. The mother informed us that he had been done, but she took a flannel and hot water immedi- ately, and rubbed the arm well, so that it never took. I did not ascertain whether he received a certificate of successful vaccination."

It seems that there were in all sixty deaths from small-pox up to the end of March,—forty males, and twenty females. It is significant that with regard to the men employed at Dallam forge which is near to the lope Hospitalcthe proportion of those who have been infected with the disease is 4.3 percent., as compared with 14 at Bewsey forge which is further Away. This, as Dr. Gornall says, seems to p 'int strongly to aerial conveyance of the disease, especially us it has been noted that at the time the greatest number of cases occurred at Dallam the wind was blowing from the hospital to the forge. It certainly shows pretty clearly that the centre of a populous district is not the place I for e. small-pox hospital.

It. will not be any particular satisfaction to the , person who is al ways spoken of as the "already 0 verhurdeued ratepayer," to know that the epidemic had, up to the end of March which does not by any means close the account, caused an extra expendi- tur6 of £7,924 7s. sd.

Vat considerate friends of the poor the Tories , are ! Only they have a queer way of showing their 'sympathy sometimes, especially when the poor man does not happen to have a vote. The Warrington Board of Guardians, for instance, is almost exclu- sively composed of Tories, and so far as Warrington itself is concerned there is not a single Liberal on it. Now, on Wednesday, this Board of Guardians was asked to show just a little consideration to the poor people under its charge. Everybody knows that one of the most humiliating things about workhou,e life, especially for the decent poor, is the wearing of a conspicuous and unmistakeable uniform. This is the badge of degradation which the poor old man or woman who have been forced isco the workhouse perhaps through no fault of their own, most shrink from. The laceration of feeling caused by a regulation which enforces the wearing of a distinctive pauper's dress is so unnec- ewsary that some unions have abolished it altogether.

But not so the Tory Guardians of Warrington. They were asked on Wednesday merely to consider such a proposal, but they declined even to consider P. o.ily five members could be got to vote for such a dreadfully radical innovation. The ntotion was net rejected on the ground of cost, because it was 541 d that the cost would not be increased; and, in y case, that was a matter for consideration. And t.init cost is not a prime consideration with Tory ...,,lardians was shown by the fact that it was .I,.cided at. the same meeting to pay thirty shillings a week to a lunatic attendant, in spite of the pro- test that such an official is unnecessary, and that theie Is now a larger staff at the Workhouse than er before and fewer inmates.

MARRIAGE OF MISS RIGBY.—On Wednesday afternoon, a marriage was celebrated in the Union Church, Fred- sham, in which considerable interest was evinced owing to the positions of the contracting parties. The bride was Miss Jane Ann Rigby, Second daughter of Mr. Thomas Rigby, LP., county &dorm tr, of The Cedars, Stitton Weaver, and the bridegroom Mr. Edward Rhodes, fifth son of Mr. John Rhodes, Beech Bill-terrace, Manchester. Mr. Rigby is exceedingly well known throughout the country, and especially in agricultural ,1 eireies. Tlia ceremony was performed by the Rev. C. ' Craddock, in preserme of a crowded congregation. The bride was attired in a csstume of white ben 'aline cloth, , trimmed with Brussels IACe, and a wreath of real orange blosSom. She wore a gold brooch II diamonds, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Was Mica Rigby (sister) and Mi.ls 31'Kentiall (daughter of Dr. M'Kennall, of Bowden). Their dresses were ot fawn blue cloth, trimmed with Brussels lace. They wore gold bangles, and carried shower bouquets, the gift of the bridegroom. After the ceremony, a reception was held at The Cedars. The newly-united pair left for Devoe- shire to grata the honeymoon. Miss Rigby was the recipient of many costly presents. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY.

On Wednesday, Colonel J. 0. Halsted, R.E., ,Local Government Board Inspects, held an inquiry at Prod- sham Town Hall with reference to the application of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority for sanction to bor- row £3,800 for constructing waterworks in Frodsham township. Mr. John Ashton,cierk to the Rural Sanitary Authority, explained that the scheme was mooted- in 1890, and originated in a letter from the Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Blogg), calling attentkm to the deficiency of ties water supply. The annual cost of theacheme was esti- mated at £430, including interest and instalment, and the parochial committee considered that the expense should be borne entirely by the consumers, and not levied on the whole township. There were 508 houses on the pipe line within the area proposed. The com- mittee thought it expedient to borrow the money , by the establishment of a sinking fund, and desired to have the first payment pos:paned for lire veers, in order to allow the scheme to develop. The Bev. it. B. Blogg dr scribed the prevent state of things as intolerable, and a disgrace to the district.—Mr. El. E. Heywood protested that it would be a hardship and injustice On the ratepayers to saddle them with such an extra expense at present.—The only opponent to the scheme was !dr. James Edwards, who objected that it WaS inennilpillie and inequitable.—Mr. Charles E. Linaker reprere:iled is large number of property owners in Frodsham, Ws, strongly in favour of the scheme, and characterised Mr. Ed ward's obj-ct ions as purely selfish. —Application was also wade by the Sanitary Authority to be inva.ted with certain urban powers under the Pub- lic Health Act with respect to Frodslepn amid Ap2leton. Powers were also sought to stenel L 1,510 in the t ternship of Appleton for sewerage works. It is proposell to Alter extend the existing system of sewerage for Stockton Heath and Wililersponl, rendered necessary by the inter- s( ction of the Ship Girlish—Atter hearin the whole nf the evidence, Colonel Heisted closed the ingqify, „d promised to make his report as soon as possible. SOLDIERS AND POLICE.

At the Borough Court on Thursday.four soldiers,named Thomas Lawrelice,Joseph Little,i;klward Quinn ,and John Tinns, were M.arged with being drunk and disorderly in Butterinarkei-R., the previous evening, and Quinn and Little were former charged with, assaulting Sergeant Taylor and Constable Barnett (27). Sergeant Turner said he was in company with P G. Leithwood in Butter. market-street, when Lawrence came to them and said they need not w atch them, as they were going to stop when they were. The others across the road were pas- sing remarks about the sergeant. He and the constable went across to them and told them to move away. Some other soldiers then closed round them, and defied them to remove there. A large crowd gathered round and the soldiers took their belts off. Quinn afterwards struck him a violent blow on the head. A scuffle en- siued in which P.C. Barnett, who came up when he beard the whistle, was also struck. At the Police Sta- tion, Quinn was very violent, ind his boots had to be taken off. Tiring was brought to the Policti Station by P.C. Barnett (31). After evidence by Inspector Spinks, Barnett, Leithwood, and Sergeant William Bickie, who assisted the police to take the men into custody, the magistrates sent Quinn to gaol for one month hard labour; Lawrence and Little were fined ss. and costs each, and Tinns was fined 53. including costs.

From the evidence of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) it appears that Mrs. Taylor sent her daughter to Mr.Woods' grocer, Horsemarket-st., for some groceries, add put the money with the order in a I purse. The girl, who is said to be of weak intellectovas passing the steps of Guest's tannery, when the prisoner snatched from her hand the purse containing ss. 33. in money. WARRINOTON V. SEFTON.—Quite 4,000 spectators were present at Sefton Park on Saturday, when the above teams met in their first engagement this season. War- riugton won the toss, and were first represented by Messrs. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield. The wicket was all in 'favour of run getting, and whilst Oakley opened with a couple of maidens, F. Jones was treated lightly, and thrice in quick succession did J. J. Crosfield place him to the boundary. Runs were piled on at a rapid pace, and at 33 Rees took the ball from the amateur. Runs Came just as freely from the new trundler, and at 65 Edwards tried to effect a separation. It was left to Oakley to accomplisla the trick, for at 71 J. J. Crosfield placed one in the hands of Stubbs at point. Sugg scored a boundary off the first ball he received, but Edwards had his revenge by bowling down his off stump two deliveries later. With R. Smith joining Crosfield runs were notched at a rapid pace, especially by the initial batsman, and quickly passing his fifty, the hundred was sent up after nearly an hour's play. Three runs later Smith was completely beaten by Oakley, but Clarke rapidly made nine, and then was bowled by a ball from Edwards, which took the off stump. Clark was easily snapped at the wicket, whilst the next to leave was S. M. Crosfield, who had made 74 out of 121 In fine style' without the least semblance of a chance, and included in which were a five and ten fours. Voisey was also snapped at the wicket, but an excellent stand was forthcoming when Reynolds and Podmore became associated. The former played steadily, but the last corner had several narrow escapes in his opening essay. However when he did settle down, some bril- liant hitting was seen. Thrice in one over did he drive Oakley over the sight board, and after he and Reynolds had put 56 on the eight wicket, Oakley brought off a fine catch at third man, Podmore having played fine cricket fur his 33. Bell was badly run out, and when everyone had predicted an early finish, Bolton stayed with Reynolds until the total had reached 203, when Smith deemed it advisable to apply the closure. Sefton concluded with 137.

, ' The twenty-sixth annual .festival, which watt commenced on Friday evening, was brought •to a conclusion on Saturday afternoon in the Sports Field, et Farnworth. Althotigh the programme did not include so many events-arrion some previous . occaeions there were 400 entries or about thirty in .eXcesi of last year. The generosity of the Commit- tee in offering prizes of the aggregate value of £2OO no doubt contributed to such a gratifying ' result. There was no great champion of the path engaged, but Many of .those competing arc rapidly reaching the front rank, and the various contests were . full of interest. Brilliant weather prevailed and the •special trains arranged by the railway companies and the coaches-of the local cab proprietors were crowded. It ass estimated , that five thousand spectators were present at, three o'clock, half-an-hour after the sports commenced... The grand stand, reserved for subscribers, was well filled. The :adies predonticated and the rich arid varied colour of their attire gave the stand quite a picturesque appearance. The Mayor (Alderman Gossagt), who is president of the club, and the Mayoress were present dinette the whole of the proceedings, The pleasure of the spectators was much enhanced by the clever performs neem of Gnssage'sSoa p Work's Prize Band, under the leadership of Mr. John Brady. . In one respect Widnes Sports have always enjoyed an .enviable.popelatitV. The admirable manner in which Ithey are coeducted has always brought forthenconiums of praise and this yra.r was en exception to the rule. The ernunde were admirably arrauge.d for . the mirpose and the punctuality with schich each race wins run to time was a highly commendable feature. A dist of the • officials may be apProprilittly inserted here :—Judges : Messrs. T. W. Grace (N.C.A.A.), C. E. Barlow, J. A. Edwards, and Major Wariehig ; Clerks' of the course : Messes. H. Auer, A. Carey, 1. Carr, J. li. Crossley, ' Stuart D.,ocon, Dr, Edwardee-J-L. Higgins, W. H. Long. ton, H. S. 'fi in inis ; Pield Moan( e Committee : Messrs. W. •S. Collander, T. C. Haddock, and J. P. Fraser ; • handicapper, official timelfeeper, and referee : Walter Platt ; starter • J. Wilkinsen •, hen. secret try': George E. Sayce ; secretary : James Welter Dayies. 'While all conspicuously did tlreir duty, a epecial word may ho said for the energetic and hard working secretary, Mr. Davies who. laboured uttwearyingly for the success of the festival. . • The, sprint race *as as popular - as, ever. Fifty-three entriee for the 12,0 yards hendicapetticessitated the rote being run off in nine heats-end two trial heats before the final was reached. No fewer. than 37 turned out to compete, anti. some of hit' fit iieties were very close - and exciting, Cowap who had ruin second to Osborne in a trial heat deeisiVely reversed the running in the final rind carried off a handsome prize werth ten guineas. For the half mile handicap for which 21 had entered, there was a field of thirteen not more than half of - whom , finished, Nancarriow winning easily. 'the same athlete also carried away the mile handicap in easy fashion from seven opponents. The bicycle races produced the most interest and excitement. For the mile handicap there were 25 entries, and 21 competed in three heats. Un- fortunately it was not carried through witheut mishap. There were no fewer than four "spills" brought about through:the unevenness oh the ground -at one of the corners, where a footeath croesee the. field. The retie was theught to be to a great extent a match between D. Dagleish of Widnes C.C., slid A. E. Barlow of Anfield 8.0 , son of Me C. E. Bellow, one of the vice presiderits and most earnest .supporters-of the club. Unluckily' both came to grief and Dagleish was somewhat severely shaken. In the end, Bellien of Warrington, who rode a splendid race, both in his heat and in the final, carried off the first prize by four yards. There was an exceed- ingly close finish for the second plane, and Sherratt who was leading coining into the straight thought he had secured the position, hut the judges gave the verdict against him by six inches. • Out of 19 entries for the three miles hires ele Lan:lir:an nine turned out and there . was some grand racing: Eventually in the last lap, Bailey, who was conceding long distances all round, forged eplendidly aim id, ailli eventually won comfort- ably ,by 25 yards. ' There was a severe struggle for second place. A new feature and one which caused much amusement was the three-quarter mile steeple- chase. The Witeejtime was both--wide and deep' and not one of the eight competitors successfully negotiated it and their gay end scanty garments had lest their shimmering sheen long before the end was reached. The one milo'scratch race was Carried off by F. 0. Bacon, who earlier In the afternoon had won a thousand yard rare at Salford. He arrieed by train just as the men were toeing the mark, and for some time it was doubt- ful if he would he allowed to start. Fowler. was die only man who could keep near him and he succumbed at the finish by 'five yards. Wright and Kelly were .nearly a lap behind, and they had a race to themselves ,for the third position. At the conclusion of the splits the Mayoress, to whom Mr. Davit i on behalf of the club presented a charming bouquet of flowers, riestributed the prizes to the winners. FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
OVER .E 3,000 DAMAGE.
EXTRAORDINARY,IICONDITIOig OF THE FIRE BRIGADE. _

Shortly after midnight on Wednesday, informa- tion of fire was received at St. Helens Town Hall, and on Suptirintendent Rutherford with fire appli-. mutes and brigade arriving in Higher Parr-st., the pawnbroking establishment of Mr. 'Philip Stephen Corrin, No 25, was found to be blazing furiously, It is a three storey building, and although every effort was made to pr miptly subdue the fire by getting three branche a to work from the main, the roof and two floors fell in, and the place was completely gutted. The shop next door is occupied by a firm of linen drapers named Thompson,. and the roof of this building also took fire. The next premises are occupied by, Mr. jeseph Benyon, boot erg' shoe dealer, who lives on the premises. They were awakened by water being thrown , upon the building, the roof of which had also taken fire. All got safely out of the buil4ing. The fire Was subdued in about two hours, and the last fireman left the ruins about six o'clock. During the progress of the fire the, superintendent, with fireman Penketh, jun., and other , firemen, was in the lower portion of Mr., Corrin's prem- ises when the roof and firer fell in. The superintendent , saw the ceiling cracking and called out his men just in time to save them being buried in the debris. The dam- ages sustained by Corrin are about £3.000, that by Thompson £350, and that by Benyon £lOO, the whole of which is covered by insurance. The origin of the fire is not known, hut it was discovered by Police-ser- geant Strong and Police-constable Whalley, who were examining the rear of the premises and saw the flames shooting from the top storey. The brigade were about r nine minutes in turning out after receiving the alarm, , and the delay was adversely corn 'tented upon. ' Further inquiries and a visit to the scene of the fire show that some persons had narrow escapes, and but for the fact that there was scarcely any wind the whole block of six shops, which are two storeys in front and three storeys behind, might have been destroyed. The roofs appear to be open one to another, and the flames ran along the rafters of three shops before they could be stopped. In the premises occupied by Mr. Waywell, butcher, which is next to Benyou's, eight persons were asleep:, and at Mr. Hunter's, pawnbroker; next door, six persons were asleep. It was with considerable difficulty they were aroused, the smoke having got into their Ile u4es. As to the origin of the fire it is 6tated that the It as was turned off at the meter before the premises ere closed, so that would uot account for the occur- rence. , Sometimes people who pledge clothing leave micelles in the pockets, and if a ladder were to strike a bundle as it lies on tie shelf the match might ignite. The bra I damage is estiurated at between £3.500 and £4,000. Large crowds of peeple on Wednesday visited the place, and afflOrtgit one section of the people there was considerable anxiety as to the clothing :which had been left in pledge. THE SUPERINTENDENT'S STATEMENT.—A STRONG

div.head: AN INTERESTING CASE.
div.p: AN INTERESTING CASE.

Before his Honour ludge Wynne Flounces at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Ellen Mc- Donald sued John William Jamson for .£1 175., made up by .£1 2s. money paid, and 15s. for loss of time. Mr. Arthur Browne who represented plaintiff, said that defendant was a photographer at Friars Green. He sent men round the town to get orders for photographs, and the customers paid is. per week,' until the whole ot the money was paid. In the present case, cn Nov.2oth. 1891, Mr. Jamson called upon plaintiff wh3 is a widow for an order. She said that she had no one to take, but alter a little persuasion, she consented to have a portrait of her deeeased husband ehlarged as an oil painting. She paid is. per week for fifteen weeks, and had not then re- ceived the portrait. Having occasion to leave the town for sometime, she sent Is. for her son to pay Mr. Jamson. When she came home again, she went to Mr. Jamson's shop for the portrait. Mr. Jamson showed her one which had no resemblance to her husband it all. He then said that he would get another for her, but the second one was no better than the first. She then asked for her money back, but he declined, and offered to take her portrait. The cards from which the enlargements had been taken had since been submitted to another photographer and a perfect likeness had been produced. Several witnesses who had known plaintiff's liiisbend, were called and swore that it was not a good likeness of him. Mr.Jamson maintained that the likeness was in accordance with the directions he received. The Judge gave judgment for plaintiff for £1 25., but disallowed 15s. for alleged loss of time. occasioned by visits to the defendant's studio.

div.head: RIXTON BURIAL AUTHORITY.
div.p: RIXTON BURIAL AUTHORITY.

A meeting of the Rixton Burial Authority was held on Wednesday afternoon, at the cleik's office, Bewsey Chambers, when there were preeent : Rev. G. F. Roberts (in the chair), Messrs. T. Davies, Higham, llindley, W. Houghton, S. Sutton (clerk), and %V. Owen (architect).

RESIGNATION OF A MEMBER. The clerk read a letter from Mr. John Hayes, resign- ing his position as member of the Authority.—On the motion of Mr. Divies. seconded by Mr. Hindley. his resignation was accepted.

div.head: CON VEYANCE OF LAND.
div.p: CON VEYANCE OF LAND.

The Clerk presented the conveyance of land at Riaton from the trustees of the late Dr. Clark to the Autho- rity. toeether with abstracts and title deeds, and the receipt for £lO5 paid for cottage property which has to be pulled down to improve the roads. The tenants had not left, and they were still paying rent to the trust e.. of Dr. Clark. They will have to leave directly the Authority intimate that the land was wantcd.

div.head: COMPENSATION TO MR. ANTWISS.
div.p: COMPENSATION TO MR. ANTWISS.

The Clerk reported that in accordance with the Autho- rity's instructions, he bad Waited upon Mr.Antwiss with reference to the plot of land which would be tahen;from him. fie demanded £l2 as compensation, and refusod to take a penny less. As the Authority's offer was :£5, this was a serious difference.—Mr. Davies moved that £l2 be paid to Mr. Antwiss as compensation, and also for the rest of the drainage, and the motion was carried.

div.head: TENDERS.
div.p: TENDERS.

Tenders were sent in—fo—r—nTanholes, drains, walks, &c., for the new burial ground in Hollinfare.— It was decided on the motion of Mr. Davies to recom- mend to the Rural Sanitary Authority Mr.Hayes' tender, subject to alteration, with a view to the reduction Of the estimate.

SCHOOL BOARD TYRANNY. A SCANtALOUS INJUSTICE. The question of ,the certificated teachers' tenure of office is, says a correspondent of the Manchester "Guar- dian," continually cropping up. Within the past few weeks several instances of petty tyranny by bare majori- ties of small Soliaol Boards'have been Made' known. The latest instance is the dismissal of an excellent teacher because be has dared to Nil:Wiest,' his character in the law courts. A member of (Certain School Board accused the schoolntaster;of immorality. Pressed for evidence, the member &Mid only cite what has been called "the tattle of a washerwoman." Refusing to withdraw the statement he had circulated, a prosecution was com- menced against bim. The plea' of " privilege " was put in, and Mr. Justice Wright was compelled by the condi- tion of the law on slander to decide that although (aa he said) the teacher had cleared his Character his accuser could not be brought to book. The costs fell on the teacher, who, were it not fer the aid of the National Union of Teacher/, would have been utterly, unable to bear them. But at the next meeting of the Board the unfortunate schoolmaster received his dismissal, not be- cause of educational incompetency or private immora- lity,but because he had been content to permit a Member of the Board to slander him.

div.head: RECREATION,
div.p: RECREATION,
CONDEMNATION,

At the tnenthly meeting of the St. Helens Water Com- mittee on Wednesday, Alderman J. C. Gamble presid- ing, the superintendent's reports of the fires at M•Brydes worhx, at stables in Parade-street, and the above were submitted. At the former the brigade were thirteen minutes in turning out, due to not having a complete set of harness, and Superintendent Rutherford recom- • mendo:l the purchase of a new at of harness. At yes- terday morning's fire considerable chlay was experienced till account of the couplings being bully worn and diffi- cult to put together. Morris's patent c.)upling was recommended, as the brigade would be able to get on , meth better wi; h instantaneous couplings. In the water engineer's reportsthe superintendent recommended ' that the fire brigade be re-organised, as fully one-half of the present members were too old and totally unfit for fire brigade work.
Superintendent Rutherford was called into the room 'atm stated that the whole of the pawnbroking stock,with the exception of some things in the front window had been destroyed. _
Councilbit F. R. D:xon-Nuttall : How soon did you turn out.

Mr Rutherford : I received the alarm from the police at five minutes past twelve, but it was 14 nAinutes past before I could get my men out, thus taking nine minutes to turn out. 1 believe the fire was discovered by Ser- geant Strongand a police corista.blo. The fire was tnen through the roof, and the two back storeys were gone. We had a fair supply of water.

„., Regarding Wfiryde's lire, the Superintendent said they .had to use part of their own harness and part of a cart- limse harness. The 'harness had to bs put together MI pieces, and then placed on the horses. He suggJeSted that they should have collars of their own. Hs believed Gaskin kw:l3.er engineer) had ordered the collars. Councillor Hit:on-Nut:tall : Snap-collars ? . Mr. Rutherford : No. Mr. Gaskin said that snap- coLars would be too expensive. Councillor Dixon-Nuttall :• I think we should have proper pellars if, any. Mr. Rutherford : The new collars are ordered, and will do tor a while. Other things are needed more badly. I will take this opportunity toted you that the brigade is in a terrible state. We have nre him; to work with. We have no life line, and at the fire this morning I had to fall down !Tom the roof. The, hose is, in a sad state. Fully two-thirds of it i out ,!f repair. 'We have no one to repair it, and nothine to repair it with. ,One-half of the own are tctallY unfit Nr firemen, and I have to rely on fotiiineit only. We want fresh blood in the brig:lde. The appliances want looking to, and altogether we are far behind any brigade in Lancashire and any local board brigade in the country. I invite the committee to have a look at the appliances after the meeting. I came ts St. Helens with the credit of being a thorough good fireman, but I am afraid I am going to lose it. The Chairman: I think you had better make out a general report to .the commdtee of what is necessary, and in the meantime we can go down to have a look at die appliances.

Mr 'lititherf-ord : I don't want to put you to a great espense £lOO would put the brigade on a very good footing, fr the present. Councillor liurchall asked the superintendent what he would recommend to prevent the blocking of hydrants,it being stated that the school Children filled the boxes with stones. •

Mr. Rutherford said that where hydrants were situate on waste land he would suggest that they be inspected a little oft,.ner than the street hydrants. It. was decided to inspect the appliances, and the tiperintendent was instructed to report on the matter at the next meeting.

div.head: ATTEMPT TO ENCLOSE A LANCASHIRE
div.p: ATTEMPT TO ENCLOSE A LANCASHIRE
COMMON..
EXTRAORDINARY DEMONSTRATION:

Some extraordinary proceedings were witnessed on Thursday night near Burnlet. A crowd of four or five thousand people assembled on Stone Moor Common, which is over a hundred acres in extent, to protest against the notices which had been posted there by Lord Aningdon warning trespassers off the moor. The Rev. E. T. Russell, Unitarian minister, presided. Resolutions w,re passed denouncing the attempt to eviclose the moor, which, it was said, had been common land from time immemorial, and pledging the meeting to tear down all fences- which might be erected and to defend any persons against whom proceedings might be taken in conse- quence. The large posts to which the warning notices had been fixed were then torn down, and the fences round ii large tract of land.;--which it .is said was enclosed ten years a,/ —were) pulled up. After procession across the moor . bonfires were lighted, the fences arid the not lea boards being used as fuel. Great excitement pre- vailed: A large number of names were taken by the police.

THE WATER QUESTION AT EARLE 3TOWN.

Sir,—Permit me through your columns to record my protest against the, manner in which we have been served with water for some considerable time past. Some six months ago the price of water was nearly doubled, but of that I do not conspla;n ; what I do com- plain of is having to pay an inereased charge, and in re- turn tot to get half the supply we have aright to expect. If na!ice was given that the water would be shut off at a given time provision might be made. Ido not pretend to know who what is the cause of the very irregu;ar supply, hut it is quite time the matter received atten- tion at the hands of someone. Hoping tne matter will be further veutilated if an improved supply be not obtAned, and that shortly, I remain, —Yours truly, Earlestown, June 13th, 1893.

div.head: FOOTPATHS.
div.p: FOOTPATHS.

Sr.—Your remarks, or those of your correspondent, are not in accordance with the facts given before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday the sth inst. I never objected to the making of the street; what I emphati- cally insist upon is, that land many others (viz.tiarner, Owen, Hulse, J. Davies,J.Foulkes, Janion, Bate,Abrams, Holmes, Kirkham, &c.) consider it is a piece of injustice to take up tile or flag footpaths, which are in good con- dition, and will wear fifteen years longer, provided the traffic over them is only about the same. Practical men who have seen the footpaths cannot deny this statement. Take Hankey-st. off Rutland-st., a terminal street. no thoroughfare. the tiles will last for , fifty petits. Is it honest to make the owners remove them? The princi- pal streets in Crewe and many in Warrington have tiled or blue brick footpaths. My property has paid improve- ment rate for over 24 years, and that of my late father for forty years. There is property in Runcorn b.iilt over twenty years and no footpath ; this is the class of pro. perty the Commissioners ought to deal with.—Yours truly, Frodsham, June 13, 1893

div.head: ROBERT FOULKES.
div.p: ROBERT FOULKES.

BANK HOLIDAY AND THE ROYAL WEDDING. Sir,—l am sorry that absence in London prevented my being present at the meeting last Monday in the Town Hall. I did, however, write a letter to the Mayor which I thought he would have done me thelonour of reading to the meeting. Tills he omitted to do, rather to my regr Had my letter been read, it would have been seen that I am distinctly averse to any urgent public appeal being made for funds to provide a public celebration of this event. We are not in a position in Warrington to in- dulge in needless expenditure : and while I join cordially inwishing the young Royal couple all possible joy in their union, I fail to see that the occasion demands or j ustifies anything similar to the rejoicings which at- tended the Queen's Jubilee. I trust that commonsense will prevail over every- vain and foolish desire for frolic and fireworks. People are not more I. yal because they spend money in rockets and catterine wheels. Let our Mayor and Corporation send an illuminated address, by all means. That is going to suffice for other towns more important than this, and so it should be enough for us. As to Rank Holiday, it is too much "after the fir." And,besides, people will not want to stop in Warrington on that day who can possibly get away. • I hone this will be, as I believe it is, the general opinion, and if so the labours of the Committee appointed hat Monday will be simplified and shortened.—Yours faithfully, JOHN YONG& 19,Wilson Patten-st., June 18, 1893.

div.head: LEGH BOWLING COMPETITION.
div.p: THE LEGH BOWLING COMPETITION.

Sir,—When the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., gave a valu- able challenge cup to be played for in the Newton dis- trict, I have no doubt whatever that he intended all clubs to be on an equal footing; and that "bowling greens," not enclosures with more hare patches than grass, should be provided for the matches. The North Ashton Club have what they call a "green." but a " brown!" would be a more appropriate name to give it ; and the consequence is, that a player who has been accustomed to a well kept ground is entirely at sea, and is literally handicapped out of the competition. It is clear, therefore, that unless a small committee of experts is appointed to decide whether a green is fit to play upon or not, the whole of the affiliated clubs may as well retire from the contest, and give the North Ashton team the honour of winning. It is not much of a treat to bowl in a match on a green like theirs; and the pleasure is not enhanced by a company of Amazons surrounding the players, and making use of a vernacular which is puzzling even to a thoroughbred Lancashire man. I hope the hint I have thrown out may be soon acted upon; and that, should the matches be continued, it may not be needful for the various clubs to practice on half-cultivated grassland, so as to be, in some measure. able to compete on something like even terms with the North Ashton team. "If I were a Bowler, I'd rather perform On a Green that 13 well-grass'd and level; But a Green that 13 lumpy, and bumpy, and bare. Is a treat, not for men but the devil!" June 16, 1893.
PLUTO.

div.head: FESS AND FIREWORKS.
div.p: FESS AND FIREWORKS.

Sir,—l am greatly surprised to find that there was no one who attended the Town's meeting last Monday with sufficient courage to move an amendment to the pro- posed rejoicings to celebrate the forthcoming Heys! wedding. Surely, the gush that has lately appeared in the papers on this subject has not deprived the local Re- publicans of their powers of speech ! I should have liked some of our professed orators to have asked what Royalty has ever done for us as Englillimen and as War- ringtonians, that we should think of wasting our time and money in fuss and fireworks ? We don't know any Royalties, we never see them, and we hear very little of them that is worthy of emulation, and why we should stop work, and spend our money because a yeung couple across the country, to whom we are under no . obligation, choose to get married, passes my compre- hension. If the ladies of Warrington are so intensely desirous of having a procession let them lead off, and ! we will look on and criticise. Who will benefit by a local display ? Why, simply the publicans. They won't shut up, and all the part they will take in any festivities will be to draw in the cash. It looks es if a local cele- bration were solely in the publicans interest; but, sir. no one can see the sights I see, and hear the sounds I hear every week without being determined, as I am, to resist any and every attempt to play into the liquor dealers' hands. I sincerely hope there will be no demon- stration in Warrington, and if the townspeople f(linw the example of even some of my Conservative friends and do not subscribe there will be no foolish fuss or fire- works fizzle.—Yours &c.,
A DEMOCRAT.

OBSTRUCTION.—A CALL FOR ACTION. Sir,—lt may be strategy, but the general opinion among Radical workingmen and a good many leading Radical journalists, yourself among the number, and also the Manchester Guardian," is that the Govern- ment are giving too much to the obstructionists and allowing valuable time urgently required for pressing teforrns to be scandalously wasted, and hopes engen- dered by the Queen's Speech to be painfully deferred. More than sufficient margin has been allowed for debate, and it is now time that the Government should assert itself and place a limit to obstruction, proceed with the Home Rule Bill and ,get it but of the House of C. na- mons and let the Lords reject it if they will. The time misspent in obstruction is wearing the patience away bf those who certainly expected a more resolute and determined attitude on the part of the Government. The Tories and their allies want a barren session and an appeal to the country, sad the chances are in their favour of turning out the Government, from whom so much was expected and so little got, by taking matters teo easy. I have heard of holding the candle to the devil. It may be policy,but it brings neither credit nor profit, but disgust and disappointment, and 1 with many others think that candle should now be blown out and the business taken in hand vigorously. Irishmen and Welshmen, by whose votes the Government got into power, feel sold at the bidding of Chamberlaig, Henry James, Hartington, and the rest of what is called the Liberal Unionist party, and the thing drags its slow length along—the 13111. is being mutilated by weak con- cessions to the irrecoucilables and the Radical party discredited and disgusted. How long is this state of things to go on ? The supporters of the Government in the constituencies should call public meetings to protest against this wretched paralysis of puhlic work. Such action would spur trp the Government. and show the obstructionists that the country is tired of the wretched farce now being played by the Opposition. Demonstra- tions have been got up in places in favour of the Local Veto Bill ; why not demenstrations to protest against the most scandalous obstruction ever carried out or attempted in any /egislative assembly in the whole world.—Yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, June 14,1893.
CYBIRO.
