Sefton were Warrington's opponents on Saturday, and the scores were: ltarrington, 203; Sefton, 137. but thou only about half the Seften meg batted. Rwas an in- teresting game so far as individual play went. R. Smith had a turn of bad luck, for he only scored four. The lion scorer was Mr. S. M. Crosfield who knocked to- gether 74. Then Mr. W. Podinnre came out of" his shell a little bit, and played 38. This was good ; and lots of people would like to see a bit more of Mr. Pod. more.

There was very little good bowling abroad, the ground was monopolised too much by indifferent bowling. But one cannot expect great things in the way of bowling with the ground in such a dry hard condition as it was on Saturday. Sugg took two wickets for 26 run; the best bowling displayed; but he was entirely off with the bat for he only managed to gather four.

Now I got tolerably interested with the second eleven. I have a sneaking regard for that team somehow. Search the week's local scoring right through and one eAnnot find anything in the wAy oh individual scores to beat the performanzes which were witnessed at Arpley on SA t urday. Bibby. and Dutton played a game which was " good cricket" in every sense of the word, and from what I hare seen of the previous play of both men, they are deserving of some sort of recognition. Bibby ran 37 and Dutton 80, and Warrington's total came to 201.
Sefton, however, were by no means left in the dark. They had only time to play three men and they ran up 183, of that total Morrovr(not out) made the surprising score of 103.

Like that great "orb," the sun, luck rises and wanes. Su the Sankey Wesleyans are tmginning to perceive. Their luck took a walk last weak, and it hadn't retdrned by Saturday. They met the Fenketh Friends Club and were beaten by 71 to 60. The commencement of the Wesleyan innings did not encourage enthusiasm in their supporters. Jefferson and Clare were each run out beton) 10 runs were scored, and five of the best wickets were down for 25. Burton played in a Spartan like or Julius Caesar kind of way. Be did it like that till he was bowled for 161 To-day the Wesleyans tackle Widnes White Rose at. Widnes. Will fortune deign to cast upon them one of her Sunday smiles. "Lets 'ape an !
The jupiors after their eclipse on the previous Satur- day, ehoe out axain in splendour on Saturday, and for the second time this season put the quietus on the Bank Q•lay boys.

I am inclined to think that Luck when it took a walk from the Wesleyans went to stay with Wire Mill team for a time. This team met the Widnes Victoria first eleven on Saturday. The latter were not victorious any more. The wire boys ran up a score of 74 against their opponents 26. This corms as music to one's soul after hearing the despairing cries that have been raised anent the play of the wire boys. Why(re) this was so I cannot say.

I know there has been a little jealousy between the Wesleyans aud this team. Only last week I enquired of a friend who knows both teams well, which was the best club. He looked at me quietly—that was all he said for a time—and then he remarked "If you had asked me which was the worst, perhaps I could guess.' This was very uncalled for, I consider.

I see Orford Crescent and Pearson and Knowles met on Saturday. Before the game Pearson and Knowles chuckled and said to their friends, If they ever did bet to Isy a trifle on them new, Alas ! How their sunnyhopes were blighted and withered up like a parched pea. They scored 20 against 58. Five of their wickets went down without a single run ! Once a fox went to a farm yard for a hen—he was so sure of it that he didn't ask per- mission. But he never came back any more. He had been "had.' Borne junior teams ought to find the moral of this and study it.

There does not seem to have been much harmony 'of feeling created by the match played between 18 mem- bers of Pearson and Knowles club, and eleven of the Warrington first eleven. This is what one of the officials of the Pearson and Knowles club says : " The "16 " did not all belong to the P.K. Club, but two or three outsiders were brought in notably Harrison. Hampson does assist Warrington , 2nd, but as heis an old member of P.R. (last season's) and in fact is now, he assisted the " 16." We thought Warrington eleven turned out on the Wednesday in an exceedingly shabby way. You will perhaps know that C.Lawton and Griffin played on the Tuesday,but did nor come down to bat on the Wednesday. G. Clarke did net finish his innings because he had to assist at Preston and the same with Rushworth.

Lawton and Griffin might have put in an appearance, and so have helped to make a better show and given the bowlers in the "16" a trial. As it was Beaman and Harrison proved far too good for the very poor talent opposed to them. Griffin was on the field but did not bat. The fact is,the " eleven " were much disappointed in not getting their younger opponents out for a small score, and in my opinion funked at the bowling, not car- ing to make a small score.

Warrington should rot have arranged the match when they knew that tneu-would be required at Preston on the Wednesday, and the team (the 16) grumbled loudly on the Wednesday as the show made by tha eleven was a farce. Some of the Warrington men did not care about the outside assistance, but they were under the impression that half the team were outsiders which was not the case. lam now very sorry Harrison was played. It is the same Harrison that Warrington tried in the first team twelve months ago when he played for Earlestown."

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Good young men, the members of the W.C.C., arn't they? They have been making additions to their officials. Some " extraordinary " officials are : The chaplain, the curate, the lawyer, and the scribe and the Pop Can. At any rate, these are the official titles that appear after the names of certain members, on a visiting book.

Twenty-one of the members set out on Saturday for Winnington Park. When they got there they agreed to go round to Cranage ! This is very strange—so peculiar that they cannot keep away from that pretty little village. I must take a trip over there and see what the attraction is. After the party ha' had tea they returned, and ar- rived in Warrington at eleven o'clock. Another detach- rgent of the club, numbering about a dozen, went to Farnworth Sports, and had the pleasure of seeing their late captain carry off the first prize in the mile handicap.

This week I have been discussing the subject of lady cyclists, with a member of the W.C.C. I find that the cl b could easily obtain at least a dozen lady members right off hand, if they required them, but they are loth to encourage ladies to carry their enthusiasm ter cycling into club tile. There is, however, one young lady who holds a honorary membership to the club, and wears their badge. For my part I think it would be better for ladies to have a club of their own,and with the evidence I now have at hand, I wish all the more strongly to ad- vocate the formation of a ladies club.

I would also make one or two suggestions about the character of such a club. The object should be merely to encourage cycling as a healthful recreation ; and by no means would I advise the members to ge in for rac- ing at sports. This is done occasionally by female riders ; I have seen it tnyself and most confess that I could not holt) but agree with the condemnatory remarks which were made respecting the masculine, not to say unbecoming spee.tacle which the females pre- sented.

div.head: Srippgma.-
div.p: Srippgma.-
The proposed formatioW .of a swimming club for the new baths is nearing a practical state. Next Wednesday a public meeting is te be held to formally open a club, and appoint officials.

During the past two weeks the daily attendance of bathers at the baths haa been almost appalling. On Ssturday and Sunday last there were no fewer than 1,200 persons in the first class plunge bath. Constantly the dressing boxes were so full that aquatic enthusiasts had to have recourse to the gallery, for toilet purposes. The demands for admission into the second class bath were still more numerous and drams of people were refused admission.

div.head: M ISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: M ISCELLANEOUS.

At the St. Helens Gala, on Saturday, Running and Jumping Handicaps took place on the Haydock Football Ground. The two principal events were a jumping handicap for £2O, £3 10s.. and RI 10s. and a running hmdicap, 130 yards, for 2,5, £1 153., and 15s, In the running competition, J. Walsh, of Warrington. was amongst those who won their hea:-, and in the final on Monday he managed to secure first honours. At the Widnes Athletic Sports, on Sattwday, W. H. Bellian„ of the Warrington Cycling Club, won the first prize in the one mile bicycle handicap, while in the 100 yards flat race (Scratch), Webster, of the Warrington Ft.otball Club, came in third.

div.head: SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS.
div.p: SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS.
A GRAVESTONE STRUCK BY LIGHTNING.

During the thunderstorm at Llandudno, on Thursday the gravestone of the Lite Dr. Roden, in St. Tudno's Churchyard, on the Great Orine's Head, a late highly respected resident of the town, was struck by lightning and, shattered to pieces. A singular feature of the storm was that, though Llandudo itself was deluged with rain, the districts surrounding the Little Orme's Head, ahont a mile away, had not a drop.

div.head: THE' EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J(;NE l7, 1893.
div.p: THE' EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J(;NE l7, 1893.

; which he said was a check, and he did everything ,he could to confirm the he which tsbe had com- menced, by pretending that it was not a matter of pawning. He gave her the sovereign and she , placed the ring on the counter, and prepared to go. But for a moment she unleashed her true feelings. There was a quick glance at the ring; a heart pang that contorted her face for a moment; a deep agonizing expression in the eyes that aboweil the woman realized that she was not alone pawning the ring, not alone parting with a pretty trinket, but parting with the link that held the fond remembrances of all that was treasur- able and comforting in ,the memory of him who was no more. It was a painful moment ; but her womanhood returned when she detected the flowing tears, and she tried to smile as though, she was sublimely happy.

Then I saw another incident which I was assured is common .enough. A rough, half-drunken lout rolled up to the counter. He calmly took off his vest, banged it on the counter and said: " Ileyah I Clime a-hie-long my lick-hic-le pet. Conte on daisy." The manager took no notice, so the fellow stood some time blinking in a stupid way. Then he slammed both fists on the counter and bawled: "Are you shoving for this neighbourhood-hic- cause yml'll.hetter-.liic-come.'
" No-w look here," said the manager, "go out of this my friend—go anywhere,but don't trouble us. We're not going to give you beer money on that ve4t."

What ! fhb it come to this-hic. A honourablesh mut refush I Well, a-hic-hic . . . . Seems strangsh. . . . . Did you shay a honourable man was refush, Then he" stood and gazed like a stuck pig and grappled with his mind for a realization ot hisposi- non. But eientually they rid themselves of him. I was informed that such men as he, came often wanting to pawn garments they were using, but it is very seldom indeed that a pawnbroker will accept an article undersuch conditions.

_ - There is a mattter worth mentioning however which I had almost lost sight of. It is the disposal of the bundles after they have been accepted.' When the assistant with the entry book has made an inventory of all the bundles on one Counter $ a youth comes and takes them all away and puts them on the floor near a lift. By this time ealli bundle is numbered with a counterfoil number from the ticket book. When about a hundred bundles have accummulated they are placed on the lift and hoisted up to another,storey. Here there is another assistant waiting to receive them. The whole of this room is fine& with double racks about twelve feet high. Each rack will hold about 1,000, bundles. Upon looking at this vast collected pile of pledged clothing an outsider is bewildered in at- tempting to conceive any system by which the pawnbroker is able to lay his hand on any bundle in the expeditious manner in which he does it every day. For in the first' storey there are quite 7,000 bundles, whilst in another storey overhead there are 8.000 more. "The system, Mr. Blunt," said a manager to the subscriber "is quite as easy as—well as eating pie. You see we have a rack for each month's bundles, and they are fixed from the bottom according to their, numbers. It seldom takes more than a minute to place our hands upon any bundle that has come in during the twelve months, and as a rule not one bundle out of a thous- and is misplaced." Then there is all the pledged jewelry. It is locked up in a number of drawers that are encased in strong safes. There is jewelry of every kind here, and there are even pledged notes of hand.

div.head: UNDER THE LOMBARD'S SIGN.
div.p: UNDER THE LOMBARD'S SIGN.
FACTS ABOUT LOCAL PAWNBROKING.
By Linui

Go down to almost any pawnshop in Warrington about seven o'clock on a Monday morning. If you are a pious young man, with a sneaking weakness for Sunday school manners, you will learn quite a new language which will serve admirably for ex- pressing yourself pithily to the scholars on the occasion of a serious emergency—when they all protest, with angelic frankness that they know naught of the bent pin on your Chair. But do not go attired in smug Sunday School apparel ; do not go attired in anything—except the most inoffen- sively coloured and most completely threadbare clothes that you can hunt up. So surely as you enter among the crowd of shawled women, who thrutch " and vie with each other across the pavement for an entrance into the shop—so surely as you do this, so surely will they close up like suspicious oysters and refrain from bestowing up- on you any of the wealth of their rich stock of seductive colloquialisms. They will regard you as a detective, era missionary, or some other equally ill-disposed person. Go amongst them seedily, as if you were impoverished—go amongst them like a tramp who has been out of work some vests, and then you will fare well. I had no difficulty in going arnongA them in this condition. So I came in for a generous instruction in the language used by this certain class. I would publish some of ii for your instruction; but the editor says it is totally unnecessary.

Sometimes these women gently chide each other, but withal, they are nobly tender in their consider- ation of weaker ones—they are the milk of kind- ness in this respect. For instance two women met by me. One had slandered the other shamefully by accusing her of basely pawning her father's cork when he was dangerously ill, with the excuse that" he wouldn't ever require it any more—for he wouldn't miss it when he was dead." When he did die a family debate upon the matter decided that it was entirely improper to inter any man with one of his legs at large—so the daughter secretly ex- tracted the deceased's false teeth to redeem his leg. This is what caluminous slanderer said ; and now they met face to face. They went for each other without wasting any time. Yo rules were observed in the conflict—hair was pulled, faces were scratched- and blows were delivered, and at length the slanderer fell to the ground her face smeared with blood, her hair dishevelled, her disconnected utterances of rage quieted. She had proved the weaker, there was no doubt. So her stronger ad- versary sy mpathe tically picked her up—and knocked her down again. This is not meant as a typical in- stance of the kindness of these women—some of them have been made rough and uncouth enough by circumstances, Heaven knows—but soch an illustration would do injustice to them generally. After this somewhat cruel experience, I drifted into the shop, and obtained a position where I could see and hear everything. And then I said to .myself Well, a pawnbroker hasn't to work much—oh, no-- but I'd prefer something lighter; wheeling cart loads of coal about or being a London barmaid do- ing 100 hours per week. It would surprise you to see how they have to work in those pawnshops from seven on a Monday morning wail late in the afternoon. There are three counters each parti- tioned from the other. During the time I have men- tioned there are constantly 20 or 30 person at each counter, and each person has a bundle with his or her name attached. The system of taxing in these bundles requires a stupendous amount of labour. It is done this way. The manager goes to the ex- treme counter. An mutant goes to the till; another one gets near the manager with a book for entries and another one for tickets. The customers place themselves in line' ,according to their arrival. Then the manager looks if everything is right— eous a look round to see that there is no issinent danger of the shop walking off, and then screws his own intellect into an instantaneous valuing machine, and his tongue into an instantaneous repartee-firing gun. He snatches up the first bun- dle, rapidly unties it, still more rapidly looks at the articles it contains, more rapidly re-ties it and shouts to the assistant at the book something like this:--
"Mrs. Susan& Emily Brown, two shirts one pair shoes, ditto trousers, ditto socks.

Then to the assistant at the pay till, " Mrs. Susana Emily Brown three-and-six. Now Mrs. Beecher what do you want on these shoes. Four shillings! Go 'long with you. I only lent you 2s. 6d. last week."

She is satisfied with 2•. 6d., and the manager goes along never relaxing his expeditious toil,never doubtfully viewing an article, never stopping in his repartee to the personal remarks passed by each of his customers. He is a wonderful being. It seemed to me that lamming that the tale ofJophets rapidity in catchingroach at the time of the flood, paled into m artinsignificance in comparison with that pawnbroket's lightning speed of dealing with the bundles. What a boon! what a blessing! what an advantage to society in general !—I said—would it be if one of these managers could be caught and pot into a railway booking office. Then, if a man went to book five minutes before his train was due, he would have a chance of getting his ticket through in that time. As the manager re-ties each bundle a discription of it is entered in a book, according to Government regulations, and a ticket is written out for the pledge, who is also paid the amouat granted, by the assistant at the till. From one counter to the other the manager goes almost all day long, without respite, and without rest. And the hardest part of his work I should say, consists of delivering appropriate answers to the " chaff " which is given him. He has a temper as a rule, which is placid and calm,and stnooth,and imperturb- able—aye, as impossible to ruffle as the temper of the liveliest cab horses in Warrington. Fancy keep- ing up a conversation like this for a few hours each day, and never seeming to be impatient: "Here, baby ! What'll tha' lend me on this? " " Three-and-six my dear." "You are kind you are. You are the meanest, skinniest chap in town."
"So I believe." " Tha'll have to wait till thee yed turns grey before another bungle comes from Lucy Matilda ilandker-son."
" Very well Mrs. Handkerson I'll wait." "Give me five bob on it." " No more than three and six." " Gimme four." "No? " Gimme three and six."

"All right anything to please you." Probably at the same time that this conversation is going on,a group of the other customers es.e mak- ing personal allusions to the manager—pointing to his bald head, maybe, and observing, Ith ! It's gone for evermore—there'll be no parting there." Occasionally there comes a stranger into the camp. I saw one. 'She Wes a woman about 60 years of age, of a character ;, thht would be described as - seedy genteel. She stooped slightly; her hair. was grey, her face was pallid 'and thin, and showed the jaw bones. She was in deep mourning. As she entered among the crowd 'every eye was upon her—and a tinge of red came gradually into the pallid Cheeks, a light of half fear, half shame, came into her eyes, and she involuntarily shrank back to the door. She wasn't used to that business, any imbecile could see. The manager saw it, and motioned the old lady to come round to the sale counter away from 'the gaze and company of the ragged throng. She went. It was plain to see what was the matter— that deep mourning told the story. The husband had gone and the unprotected widow was taking the large slice of sympathy, always on hand For such as she, in a Christian country—Poverty and I Want had come to distract her thoughts from her grief. Her eyes dropped when the manager looked at her. She cast her eyes around the floor till they rested on a pin. Then she took the ring off hsr fin- ger, for 'Liras the last thing her friends would miss and, more, it would save her from their righteous contumely and odium. She could retain their friendship while she did not flaunt her poverty in their faces—she was all right so long as she did not offer palpable evidence ot her want. Of course they understood she must be a little pressed, but than, respectable people are generous, and will con- done a tittle fault sometimes. So she tried to smile and said to the manager: "You store things here--don't you." "Well, or, yes ni'm, we do."
. - " I ehould not-1 mean a friend of mine wonld like to-to. I would like to leave it so that she wouldn't loose it."
It was a pathetic lie, and the manager read it. He sold :
"Very well m'm. We usually give a little security on these things—say £l." "Oh 1 Well, perhaps I'd better take it—yes I think so."
He took her name, and wrote out a pledge ticket,

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Uuardians was held at the Town Hall, on Wed- nesday. There were then present :—Mr. G. Rat- cliffe (chairman), Mr. W. Houghton (vice-chair- man), Rev. G. Y. Roberts, and Messrs. R. Aukland, Win. Balharry, J. Clarke, S. Davies, W. Fairclough. W. Gill, J. Hill, A. Jolley, A. J. Jolley, J. H. Longton, J. Muir, G. Pilling, W. J. Shaw, J. Turton, and Dr. Patterson, Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk), Mr. S.. Sutton (deputy clerk), and Mr. C. H. Ward (master).

div.head: LUNATIC ATTENDANT.
div.p: A LUNATIC ATTENDANT.

At a special meeting of the House Committee held on Friday, June 2nd, Mr. Davies in the chair, It was re- solved that a man be appointed as a lunatic attendant, at a salary of 303. per week, to live outside the Work- house, within easy call. When he had no lunatic to look after he was to make himself generally useful under the direction of the master, in keeping books and attending at meals, and generally to assist in keeping order. His hours should be from 6-30 a.m. to 6-30 p.m. one bour to be allowed for dinner ; six days a week, except when be may have a lunatic in charge. At a meeting held subsequently it was decided that the quarantine be discontinued at the Workhouse, and it was mentioned that that would be the last meet- ing they would hold at the Town Hall.— Mr. Aux Lam) moved, and Mr. A. JOLLEY seconded, the adoption of the mlnutes.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY moved: an antendtnent to the effect that the resolution for the appointment of a lunatic attendant be referred back to the Committee. He had made further inquiries into the matter and had arrived at the conclusion that they diet not require such an officer. The staff of the Workhouse . was larger now than ever,.be believe 4, in spite of the fact that there were less inmates.—Met PILLING seconded the amendment.—A lengthy discussion followed, and it was pointed out that in many cases violent lunatics-were brought in and required a special attendant, and it was, also minted out that the present officials had always been expected to do the werk and it was an understood arrangement in their appointments. The amendment was eventually put, but was lost. The minutes were then carried.

Mr..Alurra asked : "Is it Proper that Mr.Aukland should' sit upon the Board when he has a son who is an offi- cial r—The CHArantax : Yes.—Mr. Mont :Oh ! lanky asked because I had been asked the question.—Mr.Ana- LAND' (hotly) : I will retire if you like.—Mr. MUIR : Don't get upset about it—it wasn't meant as anything personal.

div.head: ABOLITION OF UNIFORMS.
div.p: THE ABOLITION OF UNIFORMS.

Mr_ Wst. Gila, moved a resolution,in accordance with a notice of motion given at the last meeting,to the effect that it be an instruction to the House Committee to take into consideration the question of abolishing the uniform wormby inmates of the house. Mr.Uill pointed out that if the Board acted upon his resolution they would he in- volved in no extra expenee,and they would be doing away with what was in many respects a distressing feature in. the treatment of paupers. First lie alluded to the wear- ing of scuttle-shaped bonnets by the women. He said that now the use of such headgear at once made the worcen conspicuous—at once branded themas paupers, At the time those bonnets were introduced into the- Workhouse they would not have had much. effect. They were bonnets of the period, and everybody were them. What he suggested was, that in cases of inmates who were known to be decent people, not making a temporary convenience of the institution, they should be provided with clothing vahicis was not conspicuous. He drew attention to the fact that Sheffield and several ether large towns had adopted the- system. In Sheffield, he believed, it had been argued that when inmates were allowed out in uniform; they became at once conspicuous by their attire,. and as there was naturally, e•pecially among poorer people, a feeling of sympatikarexisting for paupers,.it was eortance enough for the unfortunate inmates to be "'treated," and consequentiy,fmuch drunkennesa was caused. Of course he did nfalt, adopt that argument as. it effected Warrington—v:4nd he pointed out most was...that when paupers did gocut with uniforms they were branded as it were—they were not welcome in any friend's house whilst they wore the brand, and: they were- regarded generally with a feeling that was painful to-a man who had fallen beneath the stress of eircumstancerk—Mr, A. J. JOLLEY seconded the resolution,, and suggested that discreti.n should he used in using the plain clothes— that the paupers whose antecedents were-very bad, and who were likely to leave the place any time should have to wear uniforms.—Mr. MIII P.: considered; that the whole suggestion was impracticable. It coact not be carried out.—Mr. TYPRTON moved that the resolution be not accepted. Mr. Hutt secoaded and said that plain clothes would only induce paupers to decamp with them.—Mr. DAVIES was in favour of Mr: Mrs motion. —The CUAIRMAN thought there could be no fault found with the uniforms; thesawas no disgrace in wearing them .—The CLERK, upoxthe invitation of the Chairman, expressed his opinion upon the subject and said he was in favour of the uniforms being abolished in cases where the people had been reepectable.—After a cone siderab/e amount of further discussion,the matter was put to the vote, and :tr. Gill's resolution rejected. Of the 18 members present, eleven voted for Mr. Turton's amendment, and five for Mr. Gill"s motion. There- mining two did not vote.

div.head: DEATH-DEALING, INVENTION.
div.p: A DEATH-DEALING, INVENTION.
WAR TO BECOME IMPOSSIBLE.

'fhe Paris correspondent of the " Daily Chronicle" telegraphs :—The much talked of discoveries of M. Turpin are beginning to be divulged, and if these are genuine it may safely be said that war will beenine impossible. The most important is a very light waggon drawn by two horses and containing two groups of pro- jectiles. With the aid of font gunners four charges can be tred off in a quarter of an hour, each of these throw. ing 25,000 missiles over a surface of 22,000 square I metres. The other branch of this appalling invention itt equally effective for navy purposes.

div.head: AT OUR LOCAL CHURCHES, WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT OUR LOCAL CHURCHES, WARRINGTON.

THE P.S.A., AT WYCLIFFE. Tne attendance at the Wycliffe P.S.A., was.on Snnday one of the largest of the meetings yet held, and twelve new members were enrolled. Mr. Pickavance occupied the chair, and gave a short address. The Rev. E. West, Haptist minister of Liverpool, also addressed the meet- ing, and based his remarks on the parable of the pearl. The address which was an Instructive one, was listened to with much attention, and received fregnent applause. Mrs. J. W. Varley was the soloist for the afternoon, and rendered two solos in a creditable manner. The meet- ing was also taken part in by Mr. T. Wallington and Mr. Malkin.

SPECIAL SERMONS AT ST. PAUL'S. Special sermons were preached cn Sunday in St. Paul's Church by the Rev. H. S. Pigot, M.A., vicar of Horwich, near Bolton in aid of Heath Side Day Schools. It may be mentioned that the preacher, who is a relative of the present vicar of St. Paul's' was curate at Winwick about 40 years ago, and removed from thence to Horwich, where lie has now been vicar fur over 40 years. At the morning service the preacher took for his text the 18th verse of the 4th chapter of the Song of Solomon, and preached an excellent sermon. .The anthem "He shall feed his flock "(Woodbury), was well sung by the choir, A children's service was held in the afternoon when an address was given by the vicar, the Rev. H. V. Piget. Special hymns were sung by the children. The Rev.H.S. Pigot. M.A., preached again in the evening, taking for his text,Hebrews, 7 chap., 8 verse. The choir sang the anthem "Like as a Father pitieth his own children" (Hatton). There were good congregations at all the services, and the collections, Including a cheque of £lO promised, amounted to, £4l.

LOCAL ORDINATIONS. The Lord Bishop of the diocese held an ordination it. the Cathedral Church of St. Peter at Liverpool, on Sun- day, when among those ordained priests was the Rev. A. A. Markham, of the Parish Church, Warrington. The Rev. James Arthur Cooil, of the Bishop Wilson Theolo- gical School. Isle of Man, was ordained deacon, and licensed to St. Peter's Church, Warrington.
TEE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC AT WARRINGTON. DR. J. GUEST GORNALL'S REPORT.

Dr. J. Guest Gornall, Sl.A.,M.B.,assistant medical officer.of health and medical superintendent at the Hope hospital, has submitted a lengthy report upon the recent small-pox epidemic to the Health Com- mittee of the Corporation. In his introductory remarks the doctor says :—"Situated as the town is on the high road between some of the great centres of pvulation, and boing a dhalting-place for tramps, who have played of late such an important part in the diffu- sion of small-pox, it is little to be wondered at that it should early have been infected with a disease which; from some cause or other, was already on the increase in various parts of the country"; but it is equally true that the alarmist reports in the lootl papers have not only helped to create a state of panic altogether uncalled for, but often, instead of helping on, seriously interfered with the caerying out of the measures projected by you for the good of the community. Criticism is an excellent thing for keeping public men up to the mark; so also to be wise after the event is an easy thing for those who have not borne the burden of difficulties unforeseen, and often insurmountable." Later on allusion is made to

div.head: THR RENIFITS OF VACCINATION.
div.p: THR RENIFITS OF VACCINATION.

Then the report continues :—" But it must be acknow- ledged that the value of the practice is put to a far severer test, when the figures deal simply with houses in which small-pox has been existent, if we have to deal with a sufficiently large number of people, and even assuming for a moment the truth of the theory of the aerial conveyance of the infection from such a centre as a Small-pox Hospital, it must be granted that relatively to the people in an area surrounding such a source of dangers those living in a house where a case has once broken out are much more imperilled ; all the more so, when as so often occurs, the case cannot be recognised as small-pox for some days after it has become infectious and no pre- cautions are taken. The records which I have seem to show that in the vast majority of cases people had no discretion to avoid contacs with anyone suffering from a suspicious illness. Smallpox up to 31st March, 1893, has broken out in 395 private houses, in nine described as lodging-houses, mostly in connection with tramps, besides occurring in two public institutions—the Work- house and Aikin-street Fever Hospital. The cases at Aikin-street will be dealt with in the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health In the vaccination census of invaded houses, we have had to exclude alt but two of the lodging-houses, about whose inhabitants no satis- factory information could, for various reasons, be ob- tained. My figures then refer to 397 dwellings, and deal with all all the people collectively, and again in the 1 two classes most important to any estimation of the value of vaccination—over ten and under ten years of age. Here, however, I must anticipate objections,whieh are sure to be urged against the reliability of this table ' as giving a just estimate of tho relative proportions of vaccinsted arid unvaccinated persons. People, it will be said, for fear of legal penalties and other reasons, have made false statements,. especially with, regard to children under their care. No doubt this has in some instances occurred, but the opportunities I have had of checking the returns on which my figures are based in- cline me to think that the correction of any errors would not make any great difference in their value. The im- portance of vaccination can-fortunately be proved quite -independently of any such'rellatsee on personal truthful- ' noes. In 397 houses invaded by smallpox up to the-euel of March,(being the total number of dwellings up to that time, excepting only seven lodging-houses situated in Friars' Green, Scotland. road, Bank-street, Academy-st., Mill-street, King-street, and 'I anners'-lane), a total population of 2,424 persons had been enumerated, giving an average of about six to each dwelling. Of these 232tt persons, 545, or 22.4, per cent., were attacked by smallpox, and 56, or 2.3 per cent. died:. Six hundred and sixty-three of them were under ten yeaes of age : of these 51, or 7.6 per cent., were attacked, and 14 or 2.1 percent., died. One thousand seven hundred and sixty- one were aged 10 years. and upwards,. and 494, or 28 per e,ent., were attacked, while 42S or. 13 percent., direi. That is to say, the attack rate in. persons over too years of age was four times that ha persons of the earlier period, while the death rates are about the same; in other words, the diminishing proteatioa afforded by vaccination as life advances is shown by. an increased liability to attack. And since the mortality under ten years of age is practically confined to the tanvaccinated, the non-increase of the death rate in,the older class, coincidently with an augmented susceptibility, is evi- dence of the power- of vaccination to ntitigate the !severity of the disease after it has ceased to be able to .prevent it altogether:"" Reference is made to the relation of the vaccinated state to the character of smallpox attacks, to the deaths from smallpox' and particulars of persona who died be- . lieved to have been vaccinated in infancy, to deaths in 'the vaccinated class-are given. Of.tlie former class the doctor says :—" Thirty-foue died whowere said to have , been vaccinated in infancy, and in the majority, the presence of vaecination marks confirmed this. Eight of these died at homesand in their cases-it has been neces- sary to rely on the statements of:relatives or the medi-- , cal attendant for tha number of, cicatrices. Unfortun- ately, though I carefully examined all, in several of those treated in, the Hospital it was not possible to , give the vaccinated state from, !seasonal observation, more especially in those brought mat low stages of their illness, when alttrace of marks were hidden from view by the erruption sin two instances,. no trace of marks could be foundsand I believe thee- kaust be classed, as doubtful. Of the 34, one had four marks, according to relatives, though' only two were seen; seven had three ; 20 had two, arts:Stour had onesand the other two! :Ave bl regarded as doubtful." Of the. latter class he saps :- "The total nurnber pt these was 26, and out ot that number it will/be observed nine were infants, aged one. mouth or less, some recently born; of these infantts,five . were vaccinated after -infections and so are justly tc4 counted tiousecinated ';, two. were done three char s, onal four days, and one seven daya, before the rash,,and had confluent smallpox; while the other,vaccinated ten days before the rash, had a modified ferm of the disease in consequence of its being done so soon after infection. By far Lhe greater number of re-vaccinationawere per- forated,"-says the report, *at the expense of or under pressure-feorn employers o 5 labour, and as some of the works concerned have been specially exposed to infec- tion, it is important to learn the experience t here gained. With a vievr to ascertaining the manner in -sthich re-vac- cination, was brought about, I wrote to several of the leading. firms asking what measures they had taken to this. end, the number of their work-peop:es and the pros portion of them who-underwent the oDerstion. They have been so kind in most instances as so furnish rris with all the particulars I desired. In some, all that was. don. was to offer to, defray the expense of having the workpeople done ;, in others definiSt) and reasonable length of time was given them to get done at the cost of the firm- after which anyone who teok small-pox would at once be dismissed altogether, in most instances sick pay being given to sufferers so loaeas they had fulfilled the conditions (this implies a coasiderable faith in vac- cination—and one that events have shown net mis- placed) !" Respecting the l

Dr. Guest Gomall says :—" The actual cost arm hardly be estimated directly, seeing that the excess of the Hos- pitals Account over the estinaated expenditure for tbe Year ending the 25th of March, 1893, includes many items really necessary, but only incurred as the time in consequence of the smallpox. The estimated expendi- ture for Aikin-st., Hospital, i.e., for the provision of iso- lation for infectious diseases, disinfection, salaries of officials, Sm., was £1,097 122. • the actual disbursement has been up to 25th March £9,021 194. 51., an excess of £7,924 7s. 5d., of which sum £4 477 4s. 4d. has been spent on the Hope Hospital; the remainder being accounted for by the large number of scarlatina patients, the building of the new iron hospital at Aikin-st., the provision of the new disinfector, and various alterations. Danny of these things, especially the diainfector, were quite accessary before, and their porehase as only bas.

tened by the occurrence of the epidemic. The loss to the town cannot, however, be accurately measured by these figures ; a just estimate would include an account of the loss to tradespeople od all kinds, of the destitution of the families of the stricken, and the untold misery into which many have been thrown. I have no figures to show the amount of outdoor relief which was necessi- tated by the condition of the poor, but many of the families of patients have had to go to the Workhouse to await the return of parents front the hospital. ST ItA.N GE CM DUCT OF A PRISON ER .

Early On Wednesday morning P.C. Robinson was on duty in Friar's Green, when he found a man named Beaman, shouting and talking to himself, and behaving in a strange manner. The constable thought it advis- able to have him in safer quarters, and accordingly he took him down to the police station, but not without a considerable amount of trouble, the man attempting to throw the officer down. He was brought before the magistrates on Wednesday, and was remanded until the following day. During his stay in court he proved him- self to be a most garrulous customer, and for hall-an- hour, while the court was waiting for a magistrate, he, in a most obstreperous manner, was deliv- ering a rambling discourse on Socialism. On .Thursday he was again placed in the box, and it was soon evident that he was prepared to deliver another of his discourses on his favourite topic. Inspector Spinks said the prisoner went in the signal boxes on Wildempool Causeway on Tuesday night, lie had a discharge from the army, but it did not answer to his description. He said he lived in Rochdale. P.C. Robinson also gave evidence. During the evidence the prisoner acted in a strange rammer, and frequently in- terrupted the officers. When asked if he had anything to say in reply, he commenced by saying he had done hard work for little pay, and would smash the masters before long, when he was stopped by Alderman Chand- ley, who told him he would be examined by a doctor. and his parents communicated with. _

On Friday morning prisoner was again brought before the magistrates. During the hearing of the cases pre- ceding his case, he frequently applauded the witnesses, and it required the attendance of a police officer the whole of the time. He was further charged with wilfully committing damage to certain fitting utensils belonging to the Corporation of Warrington, on the previous night, the amount of damage being 84. Prisoner pleaded not guilty but did not care if it were proved. P.C. Baxen- dale said that prisoner had been placed in a new cell in the bridewell. During.tbe night he broke a number of things in the cell, and wasso violent that witness had to take a stick with him. Prisoner was under the delusion that he had saved some person from burning. Prisoner excitedly " It's true, its real." Inspector Spinks uorro- I borated Baxendale's statement. Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, said that on Thursday week prisoner came to his - house saying that he was very ill. He became very sick and witness wet him to Dr. Spinks who attributed the sickness to smoking: He said that he hati come from Rochdale. Dr. Spin ks- said that prisoner was not insane but was only shamming madness. Prisoner here began a long tirade about the laws of the realm, Mr. Gladstone,, the Queen, and other prominent persons, and said that he had had three .day's • imprisonment for nothing, and he would make them pay for it. Alderman Harrison said ,bat the'', would send prisoner to gaol for a month. Prisoher•withkreat emphasis "I shan't go, I shall write. to the Homeliecretary about it." Alderman Harrison Harrison tolditien, he would have to go and a medical: man irniald train° hint. Prisoner on being taken, to the cells cri ' out with a wave of the hand." An innocent man sent to gaol."

On liunday evening a man who described hinaselft as an advance agent to Coleen's Circus arrived at the Wagon and Horses Inn and ordered a bed,eayingf that be should remain, during the week as the arena was coming omthe Tnesday. He also took.a horse and trap to the Eagle and Child Inn and said he wished to bee putup there for the week, as tho circus he said he was representing would remain the week. On Monday the "agent "'went to a local printer and said he wanted some posters. printing to advertise the circus which was to cornethe next day. He said he, was in a great hurry for the posters and visited the printer several times before.the stipulated time for finishing the work. Before the printing was half finished he came and asked for a dozen bills as he wanted them for a special purpose: He took the dozen bind tyut.never returned for the • remainder. On Tuesday, morning he left the Wagon and forces after breaafast and ordered dinner. Then.he 'meet to the Eagle and Child andisaid he wanted to go about the town for an hour in,his-trap. No suspicion had' been aroused regarding thegnntsine- ness of the man,, so he was allowed to take the, tiap. Since then he hai never been heard ' of, and several persons to whom lie gave free passes into thezirens are still waiting,anxiously to utilize them.. The matter has been placed in the hands of the police,, and; as. Deports have reached them of a man travelling about the. neigh- bourhood ofi Son.thport under similar, circutnetances, they have concluded that the man is the same-sbarper. A tin box was. left at the Eagle and Child,, and:oa Wed- nesday it was broken open and was fonndlo,3antain a number of, dirty collars and cuffs, and some female apparel.
